abstract: |
  Most people want to change some aspects of their personality, but does this phenomenon extend to moral character, and to close others? Targets (N = 800) and well-acquainted informants (N = 958) rated targets’ personality traits and reported how much they wanted the target to change each trait. Targets and informants reported a lower desire to change more morally-relevant traits (e.g., honesty, compassion, fairness), compared to less morally-relevant traits (e.g., anxiety, sociability, productiveness)—even after controlling for current trait levels. Moreover, although targets and informants generally wanted targets to improve more on traits that targets had less desirable levels of, targets’ moral change goals were less calibrated to their current trait levels. Finally, informants wanted targets to change in similar ways, but to a lesser extent, than targets themselves did. These findings suggest that moral considerations take a backseat when it comes to self-improvement.
  
keywords          : "volitional personality change, moral character, self-improvement, moral motivations, self–other agreement"
wordcount         : "X"

bibliography      : ["references.bib"]

---

Most people want to change some aspects of their personality---across adulthood, over 78% of people express desires to be more extraverted, emotionally stable, conscientious, agreeable, or open to experience (Hudson & Fraley, 2016b). To date, personality change goals have primarily been examined through the lens of the Big Five framework and the goals that people have for themselves (Baranski, Morse, & Dunlop, 2017; Hudson & Fraley, 2015; Hudson & Roberts, 2014). Here, we examine whether the common desire for personality change extends to moral character, and to close others. In other words, do people want to be more moral, and do people who know us well want us to change in similar ways?

Personality traits describe relatively stable, enduring patterns of thoughts, feelings, and behaviors that make people different from one another (DeYoung, 2015). Moral character traits are personality traits that capture individual differences in the tendency to follow relevant moral standards---essentially, the extent to which someone is a “good” or “bad” person (Fleeson, Furr, Jayawickreme, Meindl, & Helzer, 2014). Traits differ in the degree to which they are seen as being relevant to moral character (which can vary across cultures and individuals; Meindl & Graham, 2014). For example, at least in Western contexts, extraversion is not considered to be particularly morally relevant (a “non-moral trait”, for short-hand), whereas honesty is considered to be highly morally relevant (a “moral trait”; Meindl & Graham, 2014). Thus, being generally introverted does not make someone a “bad person,” whereas being generally dishonest might.

People place great value on morality in themselves and in others; indeed, some research suggests that feeling moral might be a basic psychological need (Prentice et al., 2018). Moral character traits are also among the most powerful determinants of the overall impressions we form of others (Goodwin, 2015; Goodwin, Piazza, & Rozin, 2014; Hartley et al., 2016). Thus, if people recognize that their moral character influences how much other people like and respect them, then they might want to become more moral to not only reach their own moral standards, but to also attain the reputational benefits of being viewed as a moral person.

However, there are equally-compelling reasons to believe that people might be less motivated to change their moral traits (compared to non-moral traits). First, because people appear to inaccurately inflate their positive moral qualities to a greater extent compared to their non-moral qualities (Tappin & McKay, 2017), they might see no need to further enhance their moral traits. Second, people might typically be more inclined to make changes that will assuage their dissatisfaction with aspects of their lives (Baumeister, 1994; Hudson & Fraley, 2016a). For example, a person who is dissatisfied with their friendships might strive to become more extraverted to overcome these social difficulties (Hudson & Roberts, 2014). In contrast, insofar as morality involves overcoming selfish impulses for the benefit of others (Baumeister & Exline, 1999), the perceived costs of becoming more moral might outweigh its reputational benefits, dissuading people from striving for moral self-improvement.

Further complicating the picture is the fact that moral traits are seen as especially central to personal identity (for a review, see Strohminger, Knobe, & Newman, 2017). Whereas some research suggests that people are less willing to (hypothetically) take pharmaceuticals to enhance traits that are more fundamental to identity (e.g., empathy, kindness; Riis, Simmons, & Goodwin, 2008), other studies suggest that hypothetical improvements to moral traits might be seen as bringing people closer to their “true selves” (Bench, Schlegel, Davis, & Vess, 2015; Christy, Kim, Vess, Schlegel, & Hicks, 2017).

Little empirical evidence directly compares moral and non-moral change goals. In one study in which participants selected five characteristics that they most wanted to improve, the probability of wanting a moral trait to improve was 21% (vs. 47% for non-moral traits; Molouki & Bartels, 2017). However, because this study was not designed to compare moral and non-moral personality change goals, it did not comprehensively sample moral and non-moral traits. Therefore, our primary aim is to comprehensively examine the extent to which people want to change more or less morally-relevant traits.

Our second goal was to document the ways in which other people want us to change our personality traits (“interpersonal change goals”). Because people who know us well have a unique perspective on our personalities (Vazire & Carlson, 2011), close others could shape our personality change goals---and ultimately, our personalities---by pointing out areas for improvement that may or may not have occurred to us (Bollich, Johannet, & Vazire, 2011). Consistent with this idea, when targets and informants agreed that the target was low on agreeableness and extraversion, this predicted stronger self-reported desires to improve these traits, compared to when targets and informants disagreed on targets’ current levels (Quintus, Egloff, & Wrzus, 2017). However, no study to our knowledge has asked informants about how they would like targets to *change.* Doing so would shed light on whether the people who know us well want us to change in ways that are similar to how we want ourselves to change. Evidence of self--other agreement on personality change goals would show that close others can corroborate our own assessments of which traits are most in need of improvement, whereas self--other disagreement might suggest that close others either have unique insight into our shortcomings, or want us to improve in ways that would benefit them.

Our final goal was to explore individual differences in the desire for moral self-improvement. People who have less desirable levels of a given Big Five trait generally want to improve more on that trait (Baranski et al., 2017; Hudson & Fraley, 2015; Hudson & Roberts, 2014), but these correlations have been more consistent for extraversion, conscientiousness, and emotional stability than for agreeableness and openness. Here, we examine whether less desirable trait levels are associated with a greater desire to improve moral traits, or whether, alternatively, the most moral people are the ones who most want to improve their moral traits (i.e., that virtue begets virtue in the moral domain).

```{r general setup,include=F}
# Other analysis functions
IRR <- function(trait,informant){
  mod1 <- lmer(formula(paste(trait, '~ (1 | targetid)')), data=informant[which(informant$numinformants>=2),])
  names(summary(mod1))
  summary(mod1)$varcor
  varcor <- data.frame(summary(mod1)$varcor)
  return(varcor[which(varcor$grp=='targetid'),'vcov']/sum(varcor$vcov))
}
```

# Method

We recruited two samples of participants so that we could freely explore the data in Sample 1, before preregistering and directly replicating these analyses in Sample 2 (see Supplemental Material for details). This preregistration, along with all materials and the data and analysis scripts needed to reproduce the current analyses are available at https://osf.io/cbxjh/. We determined our sample sizes (300/500 targets) based on time and budget constraints (and however many informants would respond); the resulting sample sizes exceed recommendations for obtaining stable estimates of the average published effect in personality and social psychology (N > 250; Schönbrodt & Perugini, 2013). We report all data exclusions and all measures (measures not included in the current paper are reported in our OSF repository).

## Participants and Procedure

We recruited two samples of target participants (“targets”) from the undergraduate psychology research pools at the University of Pennsylvania (Sample 1) and the University of California, Davis (Sample 2). Apart from minor differences described below, we used the same data collection procedures for the two samples. Targets completed an online questionnaire (implemented using Qualtrics software) in which they nominated up to four informants who knew them well, then self-reported their personality traits and change goals (described below). Within the set of four informants, targets were asked to nominate at least two people who were not current romantic partners or family members. We invited informants to participate in the study by emailing them a unique link to an online questionnaire. Informants rated their target’s personality traits and reported the personality changes they wanted to see in their target. We sent informants who had not yet completed the survey three (Sample 1) to six (Sample 2) email reminders, spaced approximately one week apart. In both samples, we used all available data for analyses involving only target self-reports (even if the target had no informant reports).

Targets participated in exchange for course credit. Informants who completed the survey were entered into a prize draw for a 1 in 10 chance of winning a $20 Amazon.com gift card. In Sample 2, informants could also ask to be entered into the prize draw even if they did not participate (in compliance with California law). Data collection procedures were approved by the Institutional Review Board at the University of Pennsylvania (Sample 1; IRB ID: 831767) and the University of California, Davis (Sample 2; IRB ID: 1328211-2).

```{r demographics,include=F}
# Add labels for ethnicity

clean.ethnicity <- function(demographics){
  demographics[is.na(demographics$ethnicity),'ethnicity.clean'] <- 'Not Reported'
  demographics[which(demographics$ethnicity=='1'),'ethnicity.clean'] <- 'White/Caucasian'
  demographics[which(demographics$ethnicity=='2'),'ethnicity.clean'] <- 'Black/African American'
  demographics[which(demographics$ethnicity=='3'),'ethnicity.clean'] <- 'Asian'
  demographics[which(demographics$ethnicity=='4'),'ethnicity.clean'] <- 'Native American/Alaska Native'
  demographics[which(demographics$ethnicity=='5'),'ethnicity.clean'] <- 'Hispanic/Latino'
  demographics[which(demographics$ethnicity=='6'),'ethnicity.clean'] <- 'Pacific Islander'
  demographics[which(demographics$ethnicity=='7' | 
                       nchar(demographics$ethnicity)>2),'ethnicity.clean'] <- 'Other/Multiple'
  return(demographics)
}
```

### Sample 1

In Sample 1, three hundred targets (`r n.female.t.1` female, `r n.male.t.1` male, `r n.other.t.1` other or not disclosed) between the ages of `r minage.t.1` and `r maxage.t.1` years ($M_{age}$ = `r mage.t.1`, $SD_{age}$ = `r sdage.t.1`) completed the study and met our preregistered inclusion criteria (we excluded four participants who were under the age of 18). Targets identified as White/Caucasian (*n* = `r n.white.t.1`), Asian (*n* = `r n.asian.t.1`), Hispanic/Latino (*n* = `r n.hispanic.t.1`), Black/African American (*n* = `r n.black.t.1`), Pacific Islander (*n* = `r n.pacific.t.1`), Other/Multiple (*n* = `r n.othereth.t.1`), or did not disclose their ethnicity (*n* = `r n.notreported.t.1`). Targets successfully nominated `r format(n.nominations.1,big.mark=",",scientific=FALSE)` informants, of which `r nrow(informant.1)` informants (`r n.female.i.1` female, `r n.male.i.1` male, `r n.other.i.1` other or not disclosed) between the ages of `r minage.i.1` and `r maxage.i.1` years ($M_{age}$ = `r mage.i.1`, $SD_{age}$ = `r sdage.i.1`) completed the study (response rate = `r 100*round((nrow(informant.1)/n.nominations.1),2)`%). Most targets (*n* = `r nrow(dat.1[which(dat.1$numinformants>=1),])`) had at least one informant; of these, `r nrow(dat.1[which(dat.1$numinformants>=2),])` targets had two or more informants. Most informants reported being friends of the target (*n* = `r friends.1`), followed by parents (*n* = `r parent.1`), current romantic partners (*n* = `r currentromantic.1`), siblings (*n* = `r sibling.1`), other family members (*n* = `r otherfamily.1`), other (*n* = `r other.1`), ex-romantic partners (*n* = `r exromantic.1`), and co-workers (*n* = `r coworker.1`). On average, informants reported having known their targets for `r round(mean(nominations.1$it.yearsknown,na.rm=T),2)` years (SD = `r round(sd(nominations.1$it.yearsknown,na.rm=T),2)`). Following our preregistered stopping rules, we ended data collection for targets when 300 targets (who met our inclusion criteria) completed the study, and ended data collection for informants one week after the third email reminder had been sent to the last informants who were nominated.

### Sample 2

Because informant response rates were lower in Sample 2, we deviated from our preregistered sampling plan by 1) sending three more email reminders to informants nominated by the first 300 targets and 2) recruiting 200 more targets (prior to analyzing the Sample 2 data). Thus, Sample 2 comprised five hundred targets (`r n.female.t.2` female, `r n.male.t.2` male, `r n.other.t.2` other or not disclosed) between the ages of `r minage.t.2` and `r maxage.t.2` years ($M_{age}$ = `r mage.t.2`, $SD_{age}$ = `r sdage.t.2`) who completed the study and met our preregistered inclusion criteria (only participants over the age of 18 were able to sign up for the study, so none were excluded). Targets identified as White/Caucasian (*n* = `r n.white.t.2`), Asian (*n* = `r n.asian.t.2`), Hispanic/Latino (*n* = `r n.hispanic.t.2`), Black/African American (*n* = `r n.black.t.2`), Pacific Islander (*n* = `r n.pacific.t.2`), Other/Multiple (*n* = `r n.othereth.t.2`), or did not disclose their ethnicity (*n* = `r n.notreported.t.2`). Targets successfully nominated `r format(n.nominations.2,big.mark=",",scientific=FALSE)` informants, of which `r nrow(informant.2)` informants (`r n.female.i.2` female, `r n.male.i.2` male, `r n.other.i.2` other or not disclosed) between the ages of `r minage.i.2` and `r maxage.i.2` years ($M_{age}$ = `r mage.i.2`, $SD_{age}$ = `r sdage.i.2`) completed the study (response rate = `r 100*round((nrow(informant.2)/n.nominations.2),2)`%). Most targets (*n* = `r nrow(dat.2[which(dat.2$numinformants>=1),])`) had at least one informant; of these, `r nrow(dat.2[which(dat.2$numinformants>=2),])` targets had two or more informants. Most informants reported being friends of the target (*n* = `r friends.2`), followed by parents (*n* = `r parent.2`), current romantic partners (*n* = `r currentromantic.2`), siblings (*n* = `r sibling.2`), other family members (*n* = `r otherfamily.2`), other (*n* = `r other.2`), ex-romantic partners (*n* = `r exromantic.2`), and co-workers (*n* = `r coworker.2`). On average, informants reported having known their targets for `r round(mean(nominations.2$it.yearsknown,na.rm=T),2)` years (SD = `r round(sd(nominations.2$it.yearsknown,na.rm=T),2)`). We ended data collection one week after we sent the third email reminder to the informants who were nominated by the last 200 targets.

## Measures

Targets and informants rated targets’ current standing on 21 personality traits, and reported the extent to which they wanted the target to change each of these traits, using the following measures.

### Personality traits

#### Big Five facets

The Big Five Inventory-2 (BFI-2; Soto & John, 2017) measures fifteen facets (4 items each) of the Big Five personality domains: extraversion (sociability, assertiveness, energy level), agreeableness (compassion, respectfulness, trust), conscientiousness (organization, productiveness, responsibility), negative emotionality (anxiety, depression, emotional volatility), and open-mindedness (intellectual curiosity, aesthetic sensitivity, creative imagination). We also assessed an additional facet of Negative Emotionality (Anger), using two items from the Big Five Aspects Scale (DeYoung, Quilty, & Peterson, 2007; “Gets angry easily” and “Is not easily annoyed” [r]). Targets rated the extent to which they agreed with 62 statements (e.g., “I am someone who is outgoing, sociable”), on a 5-point scale (1 = *disagree strongly*, 5 = *agree strongly*). Informants rated the extent to which they agreed with the same statements about the target (e.g., “[target’s name] is someone who is outgoing, sociable”). We dropped one item from the Aesthetic Sensitivity measure (“Values art and beauty”) for reasons described below.

#### Moral characteristics questionnaire

The BFI-2 contains some morally relevant content, especially for the Agreeableness (e.g., “Is helpful and unselfish with others”) and Conscientiousness (e.g., “Is reliable, can always be counted on”) domains. However, other aspects of moral character are not well-captured by the BFI-2. Thus, we used the Moral Characteristics Questionnaire (MCQ; Prentice, Furr, & Hawkins, in prep) to measure general morality (e.g., “I am a person of strong moral character”; 4 items), as well as the specific domains of honesty (e.g., “I consistently tell the truth”), fairness (e.g., “I treat people fairly”), loyalty (e.g., “I shift my loyalties easily” [r]), and purity (“I would say that I’m a wholesome person, relatively ‘pure’”; 2 items per domain). Targets and informants rated the extent to which they agreed with such statements about the target, on a 5-point scale (1 = *strongly disagree*, 5 = *strongly agree*).

The original measures included two additional items for each domain (i.e., six items for general morality and four items for each of the other domains). However, whereas all but one of the BFI-2 items describe current tendencies, two items from each of the MCQ scales captured values and moral strivings (e.g., “I don’t believe that honesty is that important”, “I want to be honest even when it’s hard”). As described in the Sample 2 preregistration, to avoid a confound when examining the correlation between traits and change goals (which, by definition, capture strivings), we dropped the MCQ items that captured values and strivings (and the “Values art and beauty” BFI-2 item), and only included the items that described current tendencies (e.g., “I tend to act morally”) and overall self-perceptions (e.g., “I am an honest person”).

The MCQ also contains measures of compassion and respectfulness, but because the BFI-2 already contained measures of compassion and respectfulness, we only used the general morality, honesty, fairness, loyalty, and purity measures from the MCQ in our analyses.

### Personality change goals
#### Change goals scale
We measured change goals by modifying two items for each of the 21 personality traits (16 Big Five facets and 5 MCQ domains) described above. Following Hudson and Roberts (2014), we reworded the instructions, items, and response scales in terms of how much targets and informants wanted the target to change each personality trait (see codebook in the OSF repository for full item wordings). For example, “I am someone who is helpful and unselfish with others” was reworded to “I want to be helpful and unselfish with others” (self-report) or “I want [target’s name] to be helpful and unselfish with others” (informant-report), with response options indicating the magnitude and direction of the desired changes (--2 = *much less than I currently am*, --1 = *less than I currently am*, 0 = *I do not want to change in this trait*, +1 = *more than I currently am*, +2 = *much more than I currently am*; we adjusted the pronouns and grammar as needed for different items and for the informant reports).

We computed the mean of the two change goal items for each trait, separately for targets and informants. We also extracted an index of the *overall desire for change* by taking the average of the absolute scores across the 42 change goal items, separately for targets and informants (resulting in a continuous measure that has a possible range of 0 to 2, where 0 = no change desired on any of the 42 items, and 2 = “much more” or “much less” on all 42 items).

#### Change goal priorities

```{r top3and1,include=F}
#### Summarize top 3 ####

summarize.top3.t <- function(dat){
  
  t.top3summary <- data.frame(Goal=allgoals)
  
  for(i in allgoals){
    t.top3summary[which(t.top3summary$Goal==i),'N_self'] <- nrow(dat[which(dat$tc.top3.1==i |
                                                                             dat$tc.top3.2==i |
                                                                             dat$tc.top3.3==i),])
  }
  
  t.top3summary[is.na(t.top3summary)] <- 0
  t.top3summary$Percent_self <- 100*(t.top3summary$N/nrow(dat))
  
  return(t.top3summary)
  
}

top3summary.t.1 <- summarize.top3.t(dat.1)
top3summary.t.2 <- summarize.top3.t(dat.2)
top3summary.t.3 <- summarize.top3.t(dat.3)

summarize.top3.i <- function(informant){

    i.top3summary <- data.frame(Goal=allgoals)
    
    i.top3summary.list <- rep(list(i.top3summary),length(unique(informant$targetid)))
    
    names(i.top3summary.list) <- unique(informant$targetid)
    
    for(i in unique(informant$targetid)){
      for(j in allgoals){
          i.top3summary.list[[i]][which(i.top3summary.list[[i]]$Goal==j),
                                    'N_other'] <- nrow(informant[which(informant$targetid==i &
                                                                           (informant$ic.top3.1==j |
                                                                              informant$ic.top3.2==j |
                                                                              informant$ic.top3.3==j)),])
      }
    }
    
    for(i in unique(informant$targetid)){
          i.top3summary.list[[i]][,'numinformants'] <- unique(informant[which(informant$targetid==i),
                                                                            'numinformants'])
    }
    
    # Calculate percent
    i.top3summary.list <- lapply(i.top3summary.list,function(x){
      x[,'Percent_other'] <- 100*(x[,'N_other']/x[,'numinformants'])
      x
    })
    
    # Aggregate
    i.top3summary.long <- ldply(i.top3summary.list)
    i.top3summary <- i.top3summary.long %>%
      group_by(Goal) %>% 
      summarise(Percent_other=mean(Percent_other))
    
    return(i.top3summary)
  
}

top3summary.i.1 <- summarize.top3.i(informant.1)
top3summary.i.2 <- summarize.top3.i(informant.2)

summarize.top3 <- function(top3summary.t,top3summary.i){
  
    top3all <- merge(top3summary.t,top3summary.i,by='Goal',all=T)
    top3all[is.na(top3all)] <- 0
    
    top3all <- top3all[!is.na(top3all$Goal),]
    
    top3all$moreless <- gsub("([A-Za-z]+).*", "\\1", top3all$Goal)
    top3all$TraitClean <- gsub('More ','',top3all$Goal)
    top3all$TraitClean <- gsub('Less ','',top3all$TraitClean)
    
    # order from least to most morally relevant
    top3all <- setorder(top3all,-Percent_self)
    
    top3all$Percent_self.plot <- top3all$Percent_self
    top3all$Percent_other.plot <- top3all$Percent_other
    
    top3all[which(top3all$moreless=='Less'),
              'Percent_self.plot'] <- -1*top3all[which(top3all$moreless=='Less'),
                                                   'Percent_self.plot']
    
    top3all[which(top3all$moreless=='Less'),
              'Percent_other.plot'] <- -1*top3all[which(top3all$moreless=='Less'),
                                                    'Percent_other.plot']
    
    return(top3all)

}

top3all.1 <- summarize.top3(top3summary.t.1,top3summary.i.1)
top3all.2 <- summarize.top3(top3summary.t.2,top3summary.i.2)

cor.test(top3all.1$Percent_self,top3all.1$Percent_other,method='pearson')  # .95
    
top3all.t.1 <- top3all.1[,c('TraitClean','Goal','Percent_self')]
top3all.i.1 <- top3all.1[,c('TraitClean','Goal','Percent_other')]

cor.test(top3all.2$Percent_self,top3all.2$Percent_other,method='pearson')  # .93
    
top3all.t.2 <- top3all.2[,c('TraitClean','Goal','Percent_self')]
top3all.i.2 <- top3all.2[,c('TraitClean','Goal','Percent_other')]

   #### Summarize top informant-reported priorities ####

    # Weight equally
    top1summary.i.list <- rep(list(top1summary.i),length(unique(informant$targetid)))
    
    names(top1summary.i.list) <- unique(informant$targetid)
    
    for(i in unique(informant$targetid)){
      for(j in allgoals){
          top1summary.i.list[[i]][which(top1summary.i.list[[i]]$Goal==j),
                                  'N_other'] <- nrow(
                                    informant[which(informant$targetid==i &
                                                        (informant$ic.top1==j)),])
      }
    }
    
    for(i in unique(informant$targetid)){
          top1summary.i.list[[i]][,'numinformants'] <- unique(informant[which(informant$targetid==i),
                                                                          'numinformants'])
    }
    
    # Calculate percent
    top1summary.i.list <- lapply(top1summary.i.list,function(x){
      x[,'Percent_other'] <- 100*(x[,'N_other']/x[,'numinformants'])
      x
    })
    
    # Aggregate
    top1summary.i.long <- ldply(top1summary.i.list)
    top1summary.i <- top1summary.i.long %>%
      group_by(Goal) %>% 
      summarise(Percent_other=mean(Percent_other))
    
    #### Combine self- and informant priorities ####
    top1summary.i <- top1summary.i[!is.na(top1summary.i$Goal),]
    
    top1all <- merge(top1summary.t,top1summary.i,all=T)
    top1all[is.na(top1all)] <- 0
    
    return(top1all)

}

top1all.1 <- summarize.top1(dat.1,informant.1)
top1all.2 <- summarize.top1(dat.2,informant.2)

#### Correlate top 1 with top 3 priorities ####

combine.top1.top3 <- function(top1all,top3all){
  
  top1all.renamed <- top1all[,c('Goal','Percent_self','Percent_other')]
  top3all.renamed <- top3all[,c('Goal','Percent_self','Percent_other')]
  
  names(top1all.renamed)[2:3] <- paste0(names(top1all.renamed)[2:3],'_1')
  names(top3all.renamed)[2:3] <- paste0(names(top3all.renamed)[2:3],'_3')
  
  summarizepriorities <- merge(top1all.renamed,top3all.renamed,by='Goal')

  return(summarizepriorities)
  
}

#### Correlate top 3 with top 1 ####
summarizepriorities.1 <- combine.top1.top3(top1all.1,top3all.1)
summarizepriorities.2 <- combine.top1.top3(top1all.2,top3all.2)

top3or1.t.1 <- cor.test(summarizepriorities.1$Percent_self_1,
                        summarizepriorities.1$Percent_self_3,method='pearson')  # .96
top3or1.i.1 <- cor.test(summarizepriorities.1$Percent_other_1,
                        summarizepriorities.1$Percent_other_3,method='pearson')  # .97

top3or1.t.2 <- cor.test(summarizepriorities.2$Percent_self_1,
                        summarizepriorities.2$Percent_self_3,method='pearson')  # .97
top3or1.i.2 <- cor.test(summarizepriorities.2$Percent_other_1,
                        summarizepriorities.2$Percent_other_3,method='pearson')  # .98

```

To get a better sense of which personality changes people would most prioritize, we showed targets and informants all of the desired changes they had selected from the full set of change goals (i.e., excluding the items for which they selected the response, “I do not want [target’s name] to change on this trait”), and asked them to select the top three most desired changes (“Which three changes would you most like to see in yourself/[target’s name]?”). On average, targets selected priorities out of a list of $M_{Sample1}$ = `r round(mean(tc.numchanges.1),2)` (*SD* = `r round(sd(tc.numchanges.1),2)`) and $M_{Sample2}$ = `r round(mean(tc.numchanges.2),2)` (*SD* = `r round(sd(tc.numchanges.2),2)`) desired changes, and informants selected priorities out of a list of $M_{Sample1}$ = `r round(mean(ic.numchanges.1),2)` (*SD* = `r round(sd(ic.numchanges.1),2)`) and  $M_{Sample2}$ = `r round(mean(ic.numchanges.2),2)` (*SD* = `r round(sd(ic.numchanges.2),2)`) desired changes. See Supplemental Material for a description of the order in which this list was presented.

From the top three priorities, we computed 42 binary variables that represented whether or not a target or informant (respectively) had prioritized a goal to improve each of the 21 traits as one of their top three priorities. Each of the 21 traits we measured has an unambiguous “positive pole.” For instance, previous research shows that most people want to increase on extraversion, conscientiousness, agreeableness, and openness, and to decrease on neuroticism---and fewer than 3% want to change in the opposite direction (Hudson & Roberts, 2014). This indicates that most people think that low neuroticism and high levels on the other Big Five traits are desirable, and that changes towards these “positive poles” are improvements. Similarly, our moral valence norms (described below) showed that people generally consider general morality, honesty, fairness, loyalty, and purity to be morally positive. Thus, we operationalized “improvements” as change goals in the desirable direction (i.e., decreases on facets of negative emotionality, and increases on all other traits), which were coded as 1. Not prioritizing a goal was coded as 0, as were goals to change in the undesirable direction (as very few participants prioritized goals to change in the undesirable direction; see Figure 1).

Out of these top three priorities, we also asked targets and informants to select and provide an open-ended justification for their top change goal (which we use in supplemental analyses; see Supplemental Material).

### Moral relevance


To examine whether change goals and other effects varied depending on the trait’s moral relevance, we obtained norming data for the 42 items included in our change goals scale. We recruited two separate samples of trait raters from the same subject pools as the targets (while preventing target participants from signing up for the trait norming study). Trait raters were randomly assigned to one of two versions of the norming task (for a description of additional exploratory dimensions, see https://osf.io/cbxjh/). Only the first version of the task involved rating moral relevance. Thus, the trait raters included in this study comprised `r nrow(norms.1[which(norms.1$version==1),])` Penn undergraduates (`r n.female.norms.1` female, `r n.male.norms.1` male, `r n.other.norms.1` not disclosed, $M_{age}$ = `r mage.norms.1`, $SD_{age}$ = `r sdage.norms.1`) and `r nrow(norms.2[which(norms.2$version==1),])` UC Davis undergraduates (`r n.female.norms.2` female, `r n.male.norms.2` male, `r n.other.norms.2` not disclosed, $M_{age}$ = `r mage.norms.2`, $SD_{age}$ = `r sdage.norms.2`).

Trait raters rated the moral valence of the 42 items in our change goals scale. Specifically, after reading a brief explanation of moral traits, participants were asked, “How morally good or morally bad is it to be high on each of the following traits?” (e.g., “Having a forgiving nature”; --3 = *Very morally bad*, --2 = *Moderately morally bad*, --1 = *Slightly morally bad*, 0 = *Neither morally good nor morally bad*, +1 = *Slightly morally good*, +2 = *Moderately morally good*, +3 = *Very morally good*). To index the moral relevance of each of the 21 traits, we computed the absolute value of the moral valence rating for each item, for each rater (0 = *not morally relevant*, 3 = *very morally relevant*). Then, we averaged the two items for each trait, before computing the average moral relevance rating for each trait across all raters. These raters also rated the perceived changeability of each trait, which we use for supplemental analyses (described in the Supplemental Material). Descriptive statistics for the norming data are reported in Table S1. 

We conducted analyses for each sample using the norms for the respective samples. The between-traits analyses (e.g., correlations between moral relevance and average absolute change goals) involved a relatively small set of 21 traits. This provided 80% power to detect correlations > |.57|, but limits our ability to detect smaller correlations (and therefore to draw conclusions about null effects for the between-traits analyses).

```{r trait norming,include=F}

#### Summarize means and SDs for each dimension ####

mrfacets <- paste0('mr.',allfacets)
chfacets <- paste0('ch.',allfacets)
mvfacets <- paste0('mv.',allfacets)

create.normtable.traits <- function(norms){
    # Compute means & SDs for each dimension
    mr.facets <- describe(norms[,mrfacets])
    ch.facets <- describe(norms[,chfacets])
    mv.facets <- describe(norms[,mvfacets])
    
    # Extract trait IDs
    mr.facets$.id <- gsub('mr.','',row.names(mr.facets))
    ch.facets$.id <- gsub('ch.','',row.names(ch.facets))
    mv.facets$.id <- gsub('mv.','',row.names(mv.facets))
    
    # Rename means and SDs
    names(mr.facets)[3:4] <- c('M_moralrelevance','SD_moralrelevance')
    names(ch.facets)[3:4] <- c('M_changeability','SD_changeability')
    names(mv.facets)[3:4] <- c('M_moralvalence','SD_moralvalence')
    
    # Merge into one table
    normtable.traits <- reduce(list(mr.facets[,c('.id','M_moralrelevance','SD_moralrelevance')],
                                ch.facets[,c('.id','M_changeability','SD_changeability')],
                                mv.facets[,c('.id','M_moralvalence','SD_moralvalence')]),full_join, by ='.id')

    normtable.traits <- data.frame(normtable.traits)
    
    # Add labels
    normtable.traits <- addtraitlabels(normtable.traits)
    normtable.traits <- setorder(normtable.traits,-M_moralrelevance)
    
    return(normtable.traits)
}

normtable.traits.1 <- create.normtable.traits(norms.1)
normtable.traits.2 <- create.normtable.traits(norms.2)

mritems <- paste0('mr.',allitems.raw)

create.normtable.items <- function(norms){
    mr.items <- describe(norms[,mritems])
    ch.items <- describe(norms[,chitems])
    
    mr.items$.id <- gsub('mr.','',row.names(mr.items))
    ch.items$.id <- gsub('ch.','',row.names(ch.items))
    
    names(mr.items)[3:4] <- c('M_moralrelevance','SD_moralrelevance')
    names(ch.items)[3:4] <- c('M_changeability','SD_changeability')
    
    normtable.items <- merge(mr.items[,c('.id','M_moralrelevance','SD_moralrelevance')],
                                ch.items[,c('.id','M_changeability','SD_changeability')],by='.id')
    normtable.items <- data.frame(normtable.items)
    
    # Add item labels
    normtable.items <- additemlabels(normtable.items)
    
    # Add traits
    normtable.items[which(normtable.items$.id %in% c('BFI2.1','BFI2.31')),'Trait'] <- 'Sociability'
    normtable.items[which(normtable.items$.id %in% c('BFI2.6','BFI2.21')),'Trait'] <- 'Assertiveness'
    normtable.items[which(normtable.items$.id %in% c('BFI2.41','BFI2.56')),'Trait'] <- 'Energy Level'
    normtable.items[which(normtable.items$.id %in% c('BFI2.2','BFI2.32')),'Trait'] <- 'Compassion'
    normtable.items[which(normtable.items$.id %in% c('BFI2.7','BFI2.37')),'Trait'] <- 'Respectfulness'
    normtable.items[which(normtable.items$.id %in% c('BFI2.12','BFI2.27')),'Trait'] <- 'Trust'
    normtable.items[which(normtable.items$.id %in% c('BFI2.3','BFI2.33')),'Trait'] <- 'Organization'
    normtable.items[which(normtable.items$.id %in% c('BFI2.8','BFI2.53')),'Trait'] <- 'Productiveness'
    normtable.items[which(normtable.items$.id %in% c('BFI2.13','BFI2.43')),'Trait'] <- 'Responsibility'
    normtable.items[which(normtable.items$.id %in% c('BFI2.4','BFI2.34')),'Trait'] <- 'Anxiety'
    normtable.items[which(normtable.items$.id %in% c('BFI2.24','BFI2.54')),'Trait'] <- 'Depression'
    normtable.items[which(normtable.items$.id %in% c('BFI2.14','BFI2.29')),'Trait'] <- 'Emotional Volatility'
    normtable.items[which(normtable.items$.id %in% c('anger.1','anger.2')),'Trait'] <- 'Anger'
    normtable.items[which(normtable.items$.id %in% c('BFI2.10','BFI2.40')),'Trait'] <- 'Intellectual Curiosity'
    normtable.items[which(normtable.items$.id %in% c('BFI2.5','BFI2.20')),'Trait'] <- 'Aesthetic Sensitivity'
    normtable.items[which(normtable.items$.id %in% c('BFI2.15','BFI2.60')),'Trait'] <- 'Creative Imagination'
    normtable.items[which(normtable.items$.id %in% c('MCQ.GM3','MCQ.GM5')),'Trait'] <- 'General Morality'
    normtable.items[which(normtable.items$.id %in% c('MCQ.H3','MCQ.H4')),'Trait'] <- 'Honesty'
    normtable.items[which(normtable.items$.id %in% c('MCQ.F1','MCQ.F4')),'Trait'] <- 'Fairness'
    normtable.items[which(normtable.items$.id %in% c('MCQ.L1','MCQ.L4')),'Trait'] <- 'Loyalty'
    normtable.items[which(normtable.items$.id %in% c('MCQ.P1','MCQ.P4')),'Trait'] <- 'Purity'
    
    return(normtable.items)
}

create.normtable.clean <- function(normtable.traits,normalphas,normtable.items){
  
    normtable.traits.clean <- merge(normtable.traits[,c('.id','Trait', 
                                                          'M_moralrelevance','SD_moralrelevance',
                                                          'M_changeability','SD_changeability',
                                                        'M_moralrelevance_avg')],
                                    normalphas[,c('.id','mr.alpha','ch.alpha')],by='.id')
    
    normtable.traits.clean <- setorder(normtable.traits.clean,-M_moralrelevance_avg)
    
    normtable.traits.clean <- normtable.traits.clean[,!names(normtable.traits.clean) %in% c('M_moralrelevance_avg')]
    
    normtable.traits.clean$Item <- NA
    
    normtable.traits.clean <- normtable.traits.clean[,c('Trait','Item',
                                                            'M_moralrelevance','SD_moralrelevance',
                                                            'M_changeability','SD_changeability',
                                                            'mr.alpha','ch.alpha')]
    
    normtable.items.clean <- normtable.items[,c('Trait','Item','M_moralrelevance','SD_moralrelevance',
                                                            'M_changeability','SD_changeability',
                                                        'M_moralrelevance_avg')]
    
    normtable.items.clean[,c('mr.alpha','ch.alpha')] <- NA
    
    normtable.items.clean <- setorder(normtable.items.clean,-M_moralrelevance_avg)
    
    normtable.items.clean <- normtable.items.clean[,!names(normtable.items.clean) %in% c('M_moralrelevance_avg')]
    
    normlist <- list()
    
    for(i in 1:21){
      normlist[[i]] <- rbind(normtable.traits.clean[i,],
                         normtable.items.clean[which(normtable.items.clean$Trait==normtable.traits.clean[i,'Trait']),])
    }
    
    # Convert the list into a table
    normtable <- ldply(normlist)
    
    normtable[,3:8] <- sapply(normtable[,3:8],function(x){round(x,2)})
    
    # Merge Trait & Item columns
    normtable[!is.na(normtable$Item),'Item'] <- paste0('  ',normtable[!is.na(normtable$Item),'Item'])
    normtable[is.na(normtable$Item),'Item'] <- normtable[is.na(normtable$Item),'Trait']
    
    normtable <- normtable[,c('Item','M_moralrelevance','SD_moralrelevance','mr.alpha',
                                  'M_changeability','SD_changeability','ch.alpha')]
    
    return(normtable)
}

IRR_norms <- function(dat){
  mod1 <- lmer('value ~ (1 | variable)', data=dat)
  names(summary(mod1))
  summary(mod1)$varcor
  varcor <- data.frame(summary(mod1)$varcor)
  return(varcor[which(varcor$grp=='variable'),'vcov']/sum(varcor$vcov))
}

ch.reliability.1 <- IRR_norms(chdat.1)
mr.reliability.2 <- IRR_norms(mrdat.2)
ch.reliability.2 <- IRR_norms(chdat.2)

create.normtable.traits.mturk <- function(norms){
    # Compute means & SDs for each dimension
    mr.facets <- describe(norms[,mrfacets])
    mv.facets <- describe(norms[,mvfacets])
    
    # Extract trait IDs
    mr.facets$.id <- gsub('mr.','',row.names(mr.facets))
    mv.facets$.id <- gsub('mv.','',row.names(mv.facets))
    
    # Rename means and SDs
    names(mr.facets)[3:4] <- c('M_moralrelevance','SD_moralrelevance')
    names(mv.facets)[3:4] <- c('M_moralvalence','SD_moralvalence')
    
    # Merge into one table
    normtable.traits <- reduce(list(mr.facets[,c('.id','M_moralrelevance','SD_moralrelevance')],
                                mv.facets[,c('.id','M_moralvalence','SD_moralvalence')]),full_join, by ='.id')

    normtable.traits <- data.frame(normtable.traits)
    
    # Add labels
    normtable.traits <- addtraitlabels(normtable.traits)
    normtable.traits <- setorder(normtable.traits,-M_moralrelevance)
    
    return(normtable.traits)
}
```

## Data Analyses

Most analyses were conducted using R (R Core Team, 2018); some supplemental analyses used Mplus Version 8.3 (Muthén & Muthén, 1998--2017). We used two complementary approaches: 1) the full change goals scale, and 2) the top three priorities. The first method captures the direction and amount of change that participants desired for each trait, whereas the second method summarizes the improvements that participants most prioritized. For each approach, we report descriptive statistics (means for the scale, frequencies for the priorities), and examine the associations between trait levels and change goals (correlations for the full scale in the main text, odds ratios for the priorities in the Supplemental Material).

For analyses involving informant reports, we computed an aggregate score across all informants for a given target, with two exceptions for our supplemental analyses: 1) we used all open-ended responses when examining reasons for the personality change that informants most prioritized, and 2) randomly selected one informant per target for the logistic regression analyses predicting informant-selected priorities from trait levels. For scale reliability estimates, we computed the omega (ω) coefficient for scales that had three or more items, and α for scales that had two items (using *MBESS*; Kelley, 2018). We repeated this procedure to compute scale reliabilities for the informant reports, after aggregating scores for each item across all informants for a given target. For the informant-reported measures, we computed the ICC(1) from a random-effects model for targets who had two or more informants (using *lme4*; Bates, Mächler, Bolker, & Walker, 2015). This represents the proportion of variation in the informant reports due to variation between targets.

For most of the key analyses (described below), we estimated latent correlations using structural equation models (SEMs), implemented via *lavaan* (Rosseel, 2012), to ensure that any differences in effect sizes across traits were not due to differences in measurement reliability (as some traits were measured with two items, and others with four items). For these SEMs, when there were only two indicators, we constrained the factor loadings for the two indicators to be equal, and constrained residual variances to be non-negative. Average effect sizes and comparisons of effect sizes were computed after appropriate transformations (described in the Supplemental Material).

# Results

Descriptive statistics and self–other agreement correlations for the key measures are shown in Table 1 (for personality traits) and Table 2 (for change goals). The full correlation matrices for personality traits (Tables S6--S7) and change goals (Tables S8--S9) are available in the OSF repository.

```{r create table 1 and s3,include=F}
  y =~ it.BFI2.11r + it.BFI2.26r + it.BFI2.41 + it.BFI2.56

  OPE.C.ts.it.mod <- 'x =~ ts.BFI2.15 + ts.BFI2.30r + ts.BFI2.45r + ts.BFI2.60
  y =~ it.BFI2.15 + it.BFI2.30r + it.BFI2.45r + it.BFI2.60

  y~~1*y'
  CON.O.ts.it.mod <- 'x =~ ts.BFI2.3r + ts.BFI2.18 + ts.BFI2.33 + ts.BFI2.48r
  y =~ it.BFI2.3r + it.BFI2.18 + it.BFI2.33 + it.BFI2.48r
  x~~1*x
  y~~1*y'
  NEG.A.ts.it.mod <- 'x =~ ts.BFI2.4r + ts.BFI2.19 + ts.BFI2.34 + ts.BFI2.49r
  y =~ it.BFI2.4r + it.BFI2.19 + it.BFI2.34 + it.BFI2.49r
  x~~1*x
  y~~1*y'
  OPE.A.ts.it.mod <- 'x =~ ts.BFI2.5r + ts.BFI2.20 + ts.BFI2.50r
  ts.BFI2.20~~res*ts.BFI2.20
  y =~ it.BFI2.5r + it.BFI2.20 + it.BFI2.50r
  x~~1*x
  y~~1*y
  res>0'
  EXT.A.ts.it.mod <- 'x =~ ts.BFI2.6 + ts.BFI2.21 + ts.BFI2.36r + ts.BFI2.51r
  y =~ it.BFI2.6 + it.BFI2.21 + it.BFI2.36r + it.BFI2.51r
  x~~1*x
  y~~1*y'
  EXT.S.ts.it.mod <- 'x =~ ts.BFI2.1 + ts.BFI2.16r + ts.BFI2.31r + ts.BFI2.46
  y =~ it.BFI2.1 + it.BFI2.16r + it.BFI2.31r + it.BFI2.46
  x~~1*x
  y~~1*y'
  
  all.main.ts.it.mods.t <- list(MCQ.GM.ts.it.mod, MCQ.F.ts.it.mod, 
                                AGR.R.ts.it.mod, MCQ.H.ts.it.mod, 
                                MCQ.L.ts.it.mod, AGR.C.ts.it.mod, 
                                CON.R.ts.it.mod, MCQ.P.ts.it.mod, 
                                AGR.T.ts.it.mod, CON.P.ts.it.mod, 
                                anger.ts.it.mod, OPE.I.ts.it.mod, 
                                NEG.E.ts.it.mod, NEG.D.ts.it.mod, 
                                EXT.E.ts.it.mod, OPE.C.ts.it.mod, 
                                CON.O.ts.it.mod, NEG.A.ts.it.mod, 
                                OPE.A.ts.it.mod, EXT.A.ts.it.mod, 
                                EXT.S.ts.it.mod)
  
  names(all.main.ts.it.mods.t) <- c('MCQ.GM', 'MCQ.F', 'AGR.R', 'MCQ.H', 
                                    'MCQ.L', 'AGR.C', 'CON.R', 'MCQ.P', 
                                    'AGR.T', 'CON.P', 'anger', 'OPE.I', 
                                    'NEG.E', 'NEG.D', 'EXT.E', 'OPE.C', 
                                    'CON.O', 'NEG.A', 'OPE.A', 'EXT.A', 'EXT.S')
  
  ts.it.corlist <- list()
  
  for(i in all.main.ts.it.mods.t){
    coefs <- parameterEstimates(sem(i,data=dat,std.lv=T))
    r <- coefs[which(coefs$lhs=='x' & coefs$rhs=='y'),
               c('est','pvalue','ci.lower','ci.upper')]
    ts.it.corlist[[i]] <- r
  }
  
  names(ts.it.corlist) <- names(all.main.ts.it.mods.t)
  
  ts.it.cortable <- ldply(ts.it.corlist)

  ts.it.cortable[which(ts.it.cortable$pvalue<.001),'est'] <- paste0(ts.it.cortable[which(ts.it.cortable$pvalue<.001),'est'],'*')

                                                'omega_it.','irr','r_selfother')]

HH.ts.it.mod <- 'x =~ ts.HH.M3r + ts.HH.M4r + ts.HH.F1r + ts.HH.F2r + ts.HH.S3r + 
ts.HH.GA2r + ts.HH.F4r + ts.HH.GA3r + ts.HH.S1r + ts.HH.GA4r +
ts.HH.S2 + ts.HH.GA1 + ts.HH.F3 + 
ts.HH.S4 + ts.HH.M1 + ts.HH.M2
y =~ it.HH.M3r + it.HH.M4r + it.HH.F1r + it.HH.F2r + it.HH.S3r + 
it.HH.GA2r + it.HH.F4r + it.HH.GA3r + it.HH.S1r + it.HH.GA4r +
it.HH.S2 + it.HH.GA1 + it.HH.F3 + 
it.HH.S4 + it.HH.M1 + it.HH.M2
x~~1*x
y~~1*y'

HH.r.fit <- parameterEstimates(sem(HH.ts.it.mod,data=dat,std.lv=T))
HH.r <- HH.r.fit[which(HH.r.fit$lhs=='x' & HH.r.fit$rhs=='y'),
             c('est','pvalue','ci.lower','ci.upper')]


# add significance stars
HH.r$est <- formatrs(HH.r$est)
HH.r[which(HH.r$pvalue<.05),'est'] <- paste0(HH.r[which(HH.r$pvalue<.05),'est'],'*')
HH.r[which(HH.r$pvalue<.01),'est'] <- paste0(HH.r[which(HH.r$pvalue<.01),'est'],'*')
HH.r[which(HH.r$pvalue<.001),'est'] <- paste0(HH.r[which(HH.r$pvalue<.001),'est'],'*')

names(HH.r)[1] <- 'r_selfother'

selfdescriptives[which(selfdescriptives$Trait=='Honesty-Humility'),'r_selfother'] <- HH.r$r_selfother

selfdescriptives[is.na(selfdescriptives)] <- '-'

currentdescriptives <- rbind(currentdescriptives,selfdescriptives)

  return(currentdescriptives)
  
}
```

```{r create table 2, include = F}
# Compute self-other agreement first (to be able to work with the raw correlations)

agree.tc.ic <- function(dat){
  
  MCQ.GM.tc.ic.mod <- 'x =~ xl*tc.MCQ.GM3 + xl*tc.MCQ.GM5
                 y =~ yl*ic.MCQ.GM3 + yl*ic.MCQ.GM5
  x~~1*x
  y~~1*y'
  MCQ.F.tc.ic.mod <- 'x =~ xl*tc.MCQ.F1 + xl*tc.MCQ.F4
  y =~ yl*ic.MCQ.F1 + yl*ic.MCQ.F4
  x~~1*x
  y~~1*y'
  AGR.R.tc.ic.mod <- 'x =~ xl*tc.BFI2.7 + xl*tc.BFI2.37r
  y =~ yl*ic.BFI2.7 + yl*ic.BFI2.37r
  x~~1*x
  y~~1*y'
  MCQ.H.tc.ic.mod <- 'x =~ xl*tc.MCQ.H3 + xl*tc.MCQ.H4
  y =~ yl*ic.MCQ.H3 + yl*ic.MCQ.H4
  x~~1*x
  y~~1*y'
  MCQ.L.tc.ic.mod <- 'x =~ xl*tc.MCQ.L1 + xl*tc.MCQ.L4
  y =~ yl*ic.MCQ.L1 + yl*ic.MCQ.L4
  x~~1*x
  y~~1*y'
  AGR.C.tc.ic.mod <- 'x =~ xl*tc.BFI2.2 + xl*tc.BFI2.32
  y =~ yl*ic.BFI2.2 + yl*ic.BFI2.32
  x~~1*x
  y~~1*y'
  CON.R.tc.ic.mod <- 'x =~ xl*tc.BFI2.13 + xl*tc.BFI2.43
  y =~ yl*ic.BFI2.13 + yl*ic.BFI2.43
  x~~1*x
  y~~1*y'
  MCQ.P.tc.ic.mod <- 'x =~ xl*tc.MCQ.P1 + xl*tc.MCQ.P4
  y =~ yl*ic.MCQ.P1 + yl*ic.MCQ.P4
  x~~1*x
  y~~1*y'
  AGR.T.tc.ic.mod <- 'x =~ xl*tc.BFI2.12r + xl*tc.BFI2.27
  y =~ yl*ic.BFI2.12r + yl*ic.BFI2.27
  x~~1*x
  y~~1*y'
  CON.P.tc.ic.mod <- 'x =~ xl*tc.BFI2.8r + xl*tc.BFI2.53
  y =~ yl*ic.BFI2.8r + yl*ic.BFI2.53
  x~~1*x
  y~~1*y'
  anger.tc.ic.mod <- 'x =~ xl*tc.anger.1 + xl*tc.anger.2
  y =~ yl*ic.anger.1 + yl*ic.anger.2
  x~~1*x
  y~~1*y'
  OPE.I.tc.ic.mod <- 'x =~ xl*tc.BFI2.10 + xl*tc.BFI2.40
  y =~ yl*ic.BFI2.10 + yl*ic.BFI2.40
  x~~1*x
  y~~1*y'
  NEG.E.tc.ic.mod <- 'x =~ xl*tc.BFI2.14 + xl*tc.BFI2.29r
  y =~ yl*ic.BFI2.14 + yl*ic.BFI2.29r
  x~~1*x
  y~~1*y'
  NEG.D.tc.ic.mod <- 'x =~ xl*tc.BFI2.24r + xl*tc.BFI2.54
  y =~ yl*ic.BFI2.24r + yl*ic.BFI2.54
  x~~1*x
  y~~1*y'
  EXT.E.tc.ic.mod <- 'x =~ xl*tc.BFI2.41 + xl*tc.BFI2.56
  y =~ yl*ic.BFI2.41 + yl*ic.BFI2.56
  x~~1*x
  y~~1*y'
  OPE.C.tc.ic.mod <- 'x =~ xl*tc.BFI2.15 + xl*tc.BFI2.60
  y =~ yl*ic.BFI2.15 + yl*ic.BFI2.60
  x~~1*x
  y~~1*y'
  CON.O.tc.ic.mod <- 'x =~ xl*tc.BFI2.3 + xl*tc.BFI2.33
  y =~ yl*ic.BFI2.3 + yl*ic.BFI2.33
  x~~1*x
  y~~1*y'
  NEG.A.tc.ic.mod <- 'x =~ xl*tc.BFI2.4r + xl*tc.BFI2.34
  y =~ yl*ic.BFI2.4r + yl*ic.BFI2.34
  x~~1*x
  y~~1*y'
  OPE.A.tc.ic.mod <- 'x =~ xl*tc.BFI2.5 + xl*tc.BFI2.20
  y =~ yl*ic.BFI2.5 + yl*ic.BFI2.20
  x~~1*x
  y~~1*y'
  EXT.A.tc.ic.mod <- 'x =~ xl*tc.BFI2.6 + xl*tc.BFI2.21
  y =~ yl*ic.BFI2.6 + yl*ic.BFI2.21
  x~~1*x
  y~~1*y'
  EXT.S.tc.ic.mod <- 'x =~ xl*tc.BFI2.1 + xl*tc.BFI2.31r
  y =~ yl*ic.BFI2.1 + yl*ic.BFI2.31r
  x~~1*x
  y~~1*y'
  
  all.main.tc.ic.mods.t <- list(MCQ.GM.tc.ic.mod, MCQ.F.tc.ic.mod, 
                                AGR.R.tc.ic.mod, MCQ.H.tc.ic.mod, 
                                MCQ.L.tc.ic.mod, AGR.C.tc.ic.mod, 
                                CON.R.tc.ic.mod, MCQ.P.tc.ic.mod, 
                                AGR.T.tc.ic.mod, CON.P.tc.ic.mod, 
                                anger.tc.ic.mod, OPE.I.tc.ic.mod, 
                                NEG.E.tc.ic.mod, NEG.D.tc.ic.mod, 
                                EXT.E.tc.ic.mod, OPE.C.tc.ic.mod, 
                                CON.O.tc.ic.mod, NEG.A.tc.ic.mod, 
                                OPE.A.tc.ic.mod, EXT.A.tc.ic.mod, 
                                EXT.S.tc.ic.mod)
  
  names(all.main.tc.ic.mods.t) <- c('MCQ.GM', 'MCQ.F', 'AGR.R', 'MCQ.H', 
                              'MCQ.L', 'AGR.C', 'CON.R', 'MCQ.P', 
                              'AGR.T', 'CON.P', 'anger', 'OPE.I', 
                              'NEG.E', 'NEG.D', 'EXT.E', 'OPE.C', 
                              'CON.O', 'NEG.A', 'OPE.A', 'EXT.A', 'EXT.S')
  
  tc.ic.corlist <- list()
  
  for(i in all.main.tc.ic.mods.t){
    coefs <- parameterEstimates(sem(i,data=dat,std.lv=T))
    r <- coefs[which(coefs$lhs=='x' & coefs$rhs=='y'),
               c('est','pvalue','ci.lower','ci.upper')]
    tc.ic.corlist[[i]] <- r
  }
  
  names(tc.ic.corlist) <- names(all.main.tc.ic.mods.t)
  
  agree.tc.ic <- ldply(tc.ic.corlist)
  
  agree.tc.ic$r.raw <- agree.tc.ic$est
  agree.tc.ic$rz <- fisherz(agree.tc.ic$r.raw)
  
    # add significance stars
  agree.tc.ic$est <- formatrs(agree.tc.ic$est)
  agree.tc.ic[which(agree.tc.ic$pvalue<.05),'est'] <- paste0(agree.tc.ic[which(agree.tc.ic$pvalue<.05),'est'],'*')
  agree.tc.ic[which(agree.tc.ic$pvalue<.01),'est'] <- paste0(agree.tc.ic[which(agree.tc.ic$pvalue<.01),'est'],'*')
  agree.tc.ic[which(agree.tc.ic$pvalue<.001),'est'] <- paste0(agree.tc.ic[which(agree.tc.ic$pvalue<.001),'est'],'*')
  
  names(agree.tc.ic)[2] <- 'r_selfother'
  
  return(agree.tc.ic)
}

create.changedescriptives <- function(dat,informant,agree.tc.ic){
  t.changedescriptives <- describe(dat[,tc.changefacets])
  i.changedescriptives <- describe(dat[,ic.changefacets])
  
  t.changedescriptives$.id <- gsub('tc.','',row.names(t.changedescriptives))
  i.changedescriptives$.id <- gsub('ic.','',row.names(i.changedescriptives))
  
  names(t.changedescriptives)[3:4] <- c('M_self','SD_self')
  names(i.changedescriptives)[3:4] <- c('M_other','SD_other')
  
  # Merge M & SD
  changedescriptives <- merge(t.changedescriptives[,c('.id','M_self','SD_self')],
                                i.changedescriptives[,c('.id','M_other','SD_other')],
                                by='.id',all=T)
  
  # Add labels
  changedescriptives <- addtraitlabels(changedescriptives)
  
  #### Scale reliabilities: Target ####
  
  changescalers <- data.frame(.id=allfacets)
  
  for(i in c('tc','ic')){
    changescalers[which(changescalers$.id=='EXT.S'),
                  paste0(i,'_alpha')] <- ci.reliability(data=na.omit(dat[,c(paste0(i,'.BFI2.1'),
                                                                            paste0(i,'.BFI2.31r'))]), 
                                                        type="alpha-cfa", interval.type="none", B=0)[1]
    
    changescalers[which(changescalers$.id=='EXT.A'),
                  paste0(i,'_alpha')] <- ci.reliability(data=na.omit(dat[,c(paste0(i,'.BFI2.6'),
                                                                            paste0(i,'.BFI2.21'))]),

                                                                            paste0(i,'.BFI2.56'))]), 
                                                        type="alpha-cfa", interval.type="none", B=0)[1]
    
    changescalers[which(changescalers$.id=='AGR.C'),
                  paste0(i,'_alpha')] <- ci.reliability(data=na.omit(dat[,c(paste0(i,'.BFI2.2'),
                                                                            paste0(i,'.BFI2.32'))]), 
                                                        type="alpha-cfa", interval.type="none", B=0)[1] 
    
    changescalers[which(changescalers$.id=='AGR.R'),
                  paste0(i,'_alpha')] <-  ci.reliability(data=na.omit(dat[,c(paste0(i,'.BFI2.7'),
                                                                             paste0(i,'.BFI2.37r'))]), 
                                                         type="alpha-cfa", interval.type="none", B=0)[1]
    
    changescalers[which(changescalers$.id=='AGR.T'),
                  paste0(i,'_alpha')] <- ci.reliability(data=na.omit(dat[,c(paste0(i,'.BFI2.12r'),
                                                                            paste0(i,'.BFI2.27'))]), 
                                                        type="alpha-cfa", interval.type="none", B=0)[1]
    
    changescalers[which(changescalers$.id=='CON.O'),
                  paste0(i,'_alpha')] <- ci.reliability(data=na.omit(dat[,c(paste0(i,'.BFI2.3'),
                                                                            paste0(i,'.BFI2.33'))]),
                                                        type="alpha-cfa", interval.type="none", B=0)[1] 
    
    changescalers[which(changescalers$.id=='CON.P'),
                  paste0(i,'_alpha')] <- ci.reliability(data=na.omit(dat[,c(paste0(i,'.BFI2.8r'),
                                                                            paste0(i,'.BFI2.53'))]),
                                                        type="alpha-cfa", interval.type="none", B=0)[1]
    
    changescalers[which(changescalers$.id=='CON.R'),

    changescalers[which(changescalers$.id=='MCQ.GM'),

                                                                            paste0(i,'.MCQ.GM5'))]), 
                                                        type="alpha-cfa", interval.type="none", B=0)[1] 
    
    changescalers[which(changescalers$.id=='MCQ.H'),
                  paste0(i,'_alpha')] <- ci.reliability(data=na.omit(dat[,c(paste0(i,'.MCQ.H3'),
                                                                            paste0(i,'.MCQ.H4'))]), 
                                                        type="alpha-cfa", interval.type="none", B=0)[1] 
    
    changescalers[which(changescalers$.id=='MCQ.F'),
                  paste0(i,'_alpha')] <- ci.reliability(data=na.omit(dat[,c(paste0(i,'.MCQ.F1'),
                                                                            paste0(i,'.MCQ.F4'))]), 
                                                        type="alpha-cfa", interval.type="none", B=0)[1] 
    
    changescalers[which(changescalers$.id=='MCQ.L'),
                  paste0(i,'_alpha')] <- ci.reliability(data=na.omit(dat[,c(paste0(i,'.MCQ.L1'),
                                                                            paste0(i,'.MCQ.L4'))]), 
                                                        type="alpha-cfa", interval.type="none", B=0)[1] 
    
    changescalers[which(changescalers$.id=='MCQ.P'),
                  paste0(i,'_alpha')] <- ci.reliability(data=na.omit(dat[,c(paste0(i,'.MCQ.P1'),
                                                                            paste0(i,'.MCQ.P4'))]), 
                                                        type="alpha-cfa", interval.type="none", B=0)[1] 
    
  }
  
  changedescriptives <- merge(changedescriptives,changescalers,by='.id')
  
  #### Inter-Rater Reliability ####
  
  for(i in allfacets){
    changedescriptives[which(changedescriptives$.id==i),'irr'] <- IRR(paste0('ic.',i),informant)
  }
  
  #### Add self-other agreement from SEMs (already computed) ####

  changedescriptives <- merge(changedescriptives,
                              agree.tc.ic[,c('.id','r_selfother')],by='.id')
  
  #### Clean up and write ####
  
  changedescriptives <- changedescriptives[,c('.id','Trait','M_self','SD_self','tc_alpha',
                                                  'M_other','SD_other','ic_alpha','irr',
                                                  'r_selfother')]
  
  names(changedescriptives)[5] <- 'alpha_self'
  names(changedescriptives)[8] <- 'alpha_other'
  
  changedescriptives[,3:9] <- sapply(changedescriptives[,3:9],function(x){round(x,2)})
  
  changedescriptives[,c('alpha_self','alpha_other','irr')] <- sapply(changedescriptives[,c('alpha_self','alpha_other','irr')],formatrs)
  
  return(changedescriptives)
}

    changedescriptives.3[which(changedescriptives.3$.id=='MCQ.L'),

                                                                            paste0('tc','.MCQ.L4'))]), 
                                                        type="alpha-cfa", interval.type="none", B=0)[1] 
    
    changedescriptives.3[which(changedescriptives.3$.id=='MCQ.P'),

compute.abs <- function(dat){
  # Compute mean absolute change for each trait
  
  # First, compute absolute change for each participant, for each trait

  tc.changefacets.abs <- paste0(tc.changefacets,'.abs')
  ic.changefacets.abs <- paste0(ic.changefacets,'.abs')
  
  dat[,tc.changefacets.abs] <- abs(dat[,tc.changefacets])
  dat[,ic.changefacets.abs] <- abs(dat[,ic.changefacets])
  
  # Then compute the mean across participants
  tc.abs <- data.frame(describe(dat[,tc.changefacets.abs]))
  tc.abs$.id <- row.names(tc.abs)
  tc.abs <- tc.abs[,c('.id','mean')]
  names(tc.abs)[2] <- 'M_self_abs'
  tc.abs$.id <- gsub('tc.','',tc.abs$.id)
  tc.abs$.id <- gsub('.abs','',tc.abs$.id)
  
  ic.abs <- data.frame(describe(dat[,ic.changefacets.abs]))
  ic.abs$.id <- row.names(ic.abs)
  ic.abs <- ic.abs[,c('.id','mean')]
  names(ic.abs)[2] <- 'M_other_abs'
  ic.abs$.id <- gsub('ic.','',ic.abs$.id)
  ic.abs$.id <- gsub('.abs','',ic.abs$.id)
  
  # Merge self and other
  abs <- merge(tc.abs,ic.abs,by='.id')
  
  return(abs)
}

compute.abs.target <- function(dat){
  # Compute mean absolute change for each trait
  
  # First, compute absolute change for each participant, for each trait

  tc.changefacets.abs <- paste0(tc.changefacets,'.abs')

  dat[,tc.changefacets.abs] <- abs(dat[,tc.changefacets])

  # Then compute the mean across participants
  tc.abs <- data.frame(describe(dat[,tc.changefacets.abs]))
  tc.abs$.id <- row.names(tc.abs)
  tc.abs <- tc.abs[,c('.id','mean')]
  names(tc.abs)[2] <- 'M_self_abs'
  tc.abs$.id <- gsub('tc.','',tc.abs$.id)
  tc.abs$.id <- gsub('.abs','',tc.abs$.id)
  
  # rename
  abs <- tc.abs
  
  return(abs)
}

abs.1 <- compute.abs(dat.1)
abs.2 <- compute.abs(dat.2)
abs.3 <- compute.abs.target(dat.3)
```

```{r create tables S6 to S9,include=F}
create.currentcortable <- function(dat){
  
  currentcortable <- cor(dat[,c(ts.currentfacets,it.currentfacets)],use='pairwise.complete.obs')

  currentcortable$Trait <- paste0(1:42,'. ', currentcortable$Trait)
  
  return(currentcortable)
  
}
```

```{r create figure 1,include=F}
create.perc.change <- function(dat,informant){
  
  perc.goals <- data.frame(.id=allfacets)

  for(i in allfacets){
   perc.goals[which(perc.goals$.id==i),'% same'] <- 100*(nrow(dat[which(dat[,paste0('tc.',
                                                                    i)]==0),])/nrow(dat))
   perc.goals[which(perc.goals$.id==i),'% increase'] <- 100*(nrow(dat[which(dat[,paste0('tc.',
                                                                         i)]>0),])/nrow(dat))
   perc.goals[which(perc.goals$.id==i),'% decrease'] <- 100*(nrow(dat[which(dat[,paste0('tc.',
                                                                          i)]<0),])/nrow(dat))
  
   perc.goals[which(perc.goals$.id==i),'% same (other)'] <- 100*(nrow(
                         informant[which(informant[,paste0('ic.',i)]==0),])/nrow(informant))
   
   perc.goals[which(perc.goals$.id==i),'% increase (other)'] <- 100*(nrow(
                          informant[which(informant[,paste0('ic.',i)]>0),])/nrow(informant))
    
   perc.goals[which(perc.goals$.id==i),'% decrease (other)'] <- 100*(nrow(
                           informant[which(informant[,paste0('ic.',i)]<0),])/nrow(informant))
    
  }
  
  perc.goals <- addtraitlabels(perc.goals)
  
  return(perc.goals)
  
}
```

```{r correlate change goals with norms,include=F}
compute.abs <- function(dat){
  # Compute mean absolute change for each trait
  
  # First, compute absolute change for each participant, for each trait

  tc.changefacets.abs <- paste0(tc.changefacets,'.abs')
  ic.changefacets.abs <- paste0(ic.changefacets,'.abs')
  
  dat[,tc.changefacets.abs] <- abs(dat[,tc.changefacets])
  dat[,ic.changefacets.abs] <- abs(dat[,ic.changefacets])
  
  # Then compute the mean across participants
  tc.abs <- data.frame(describe(dat[,tc.changefacets.abs]))
  tc.abs$.id <- row.names(tc.abs)
  tc.abs <- tc.abs[,c('.id','mean')]
  names(tc.abs)[2] <- 'M_self_abs'
  tc.abs$.id <- gsub('tc.','',tc.abs$.id)
  tc.abs$.id <- gsub('.abs','',tc.abs$.id)
  
  ic.abs <- data.frame(describe(dat[,ic.changefacets.abs]))
  ic.abs$.id <- row.names(ic.abs)
  ic.abs <- ic.abs[,c('.id','mean')]
  names(ic.abs)[2] <- 'M_other_abs'
  ic.abs$.id <- gsub('ic.','',ic.abs$.id)
  ic.abs$.id <- gsub('.abs','',ic.abs$.id)
  
  # Merge self and other
  abs <- merge(tc.abs,ic.abs,by='.id')
  
  return(abs)
}

create.currentlevels <- function(dat){
  
  ts.currentlevels <- describe(dat[,ts.currentfacets])
  it.currentlevels <- describe(dat[,it.currentfacets])
  
  ts.currentlevels$.id <- gsub('ts.','',row.names(ts.currentlevels))
  it.currentlevels$.id <- gsub('it.','',row.names(it.currentlevels))
  
  names(ts.currentlevels)[3] <- 'M_self_current'
  names(it.currentlevels)[3] <- 'M_other_current'
  
  # Merge M & SD
  currentlevels <- merge(ts.currentlevels[,c('.id','M_self_current')],
                               it.currentlevels[,c('.id','M_other_current')],
                               by='.id',all=T)
  
  return(currentlevels)
}

  ts.currentlevels <- describe(dat[,ts.currentfacets])

  names(ts.currentlevels)[3] <- 'M_self_current'

  # Merge M & SD
  currentlevels <- ts.currentlevels[,c('.id','M_self_current')]
  
  return(currentlevels)
  }

create.testnorms <- function(normtable.traits,abs,current){
  testnorms <- merge(normtable.traits[,c('.id','Trait',
                                           'M_moralrelevance',
                                           'M_changeability')],
                            abs,by='.id')
  testnorms <- merge(testnorms,current[,c('.id','M_self_current','M_other_current')],by='.id')
  return(testnorms)
}

create.testnorms.3 <- function(normtable.traits,abs,current){
  testnorms <- merge(normtable.traits[,c('.id','Trait',
                                           'M_moralrelevance')],
                            abs,by='.id')
  testnorms <- merge(testnorms,current[,c('.id','M_self_current')],by='.id')
  return(testnorms)
}

# Correlate moral relevance with self-rated absolute change goals
self.testmoralrelevance.1 <- cor.test(testnorms.1$M_moralrelevance,
                                      testnorms.1$M_self_abs,method='pearson')
self.testmoralrelevance.2 <- cor.test(testnorms.2$M_moralrelevance,
                                      testnorms.2$M_self_abs,method='pearson')
self.testmoralrelevance.3 <- cor.test(testnorms.3$M_moralrelevance,
                                      testnorms.3$M_self_abs,method='pearson')

# Correlate changeability with self-rated absolute change goals
self.testchangeability.1 <- cor.test(testnorms.1$M_changeability,
                                     testnorms.1$M_self_abs,method='pearson')

                                     testnorms.2$M_self_abs,method='pearson')
```

As shown in Table 2 and Figures 1 and 2, targets showed the strongest desires to decrease on all facets of negative emotionality (anxiety, depression, emotional volatility, anger), and to increase on creative imagination, productiveness, and sociability. In contrast, targets reported weaker desires to change traits that were more morally relevant (e.g., honesty, general morality, compassion, fairness). To further understand this pattern, for each trait, we converted each participant’s change goal into an absolute value, then averaged those values across participants to compute the average amount of desired change for each trait. This procedure places equal weight on goals to change in either direction (e.g., goals to become more or less compassionate both contributed to higher average absolute change goals for this analysis). We then correlated the average absolute change goal for each trait with the traits’ moral relevance scores (rated by a separate sample of participants). This showed that on average, targets showed a lower desire to change traits that were more morally relevant, *r*(`r self.testmoralrelevance.1$parameter`) = `r formatrs(self.testmoralrelevance.1$estimate)`, 95% CI [`r formatrs(self.testmoralrelevance.1$conf.int[1])`, `r formatrs(self.testmoralrelevance.1$conf.int[2])`], *p* < .001 (Sample 1) and *r*(`r self.testmoralrelevance.2$parameter`) = `r formatrs(self.testmoralrelevance.2$estimate)`, 95% CI [`r formatrs(self.testmoralrelevance.2$conf.int[1])`, `r formatrs(self.testmoralrelevance.2$conf.int[2])`], *p* = `r formatps(self.testmoralrelevance.2$p.value)` (Sample 2).

*Figure 1.* Categorical summary of change goals scale. Bars represent the percentage of targets or individual informants (i.e., not aggregated informants) who wanted the target to increase, decrease, or stay the same on each trait. To facilitate visual comparison, the traits are ordered from least to most morally relevant, based on the average of the moral relevance norms across the two samples (weighted equally). However, the analyses for each sample used the moral relevance norms for the respective sample.

```{r create figure 2, include=F}
create.top3.stacked <- function(top3all.t,top3all.i,currentlevels,n){
    top3all.t$type <- 'Self-Reported Priorities'
    top3all.i$type <- 'Informant-Reported Priorities'
    
    names(top3all.t)[3] <- c('Percent')
    names(top3all.i)[3] <- c('Percent')
    
    # add margins of error (1.96*se)
    top3all.t$ci <- 1.96*sqrt((top3all.t$Percent*(100-top3all.t$Percent))/n)
    top3all.i$ci <- 1.96*sqrt((top3all.i$Percent*(100-top3all.i$Percent))/n)
    
    top3all.t$Percent_Plot <- -1*top3all.t$Percent
    top3all.i$Percent_Plot <- top3all.i$Percent
    
    top3all.stacked <- rbind(top3all.t,top3all.i)
    
    top3all.stacked$type <- factor(top3all.stacked$type, 
                                     levels=c('Informant-Reported Priorities',
                                              'Self-Reported Priorities'))
    
    # Only plot improvements
    top3all.stacked <- top3all.stacked[which(top3all.stacked$Goal %in% desirablegoals),]
    
    # Reorder from least to most morally-relevant
    top3all.stacked[which(top3all.stacked$TraitClean=='Anxious'),'.id'] <- 'NEG.A'
    top3all.stacked[which(top3all.stacked$TraitClean=='Depressed'),'.id'] <- 'NEG.D'
    top3all.stacked[which(top3all.stacked$TraitClean=='Sociable'),'.id'] <- 'EXT.S'
    top3all.stacked[which(top3all.stacked$TraitClean=='Emotionally Volatile'),'.id'] <- 'NEG.E'
    top3all.stacked[which(top3all.stacked$TraitClean=='Productive'),'.id'] <- 'CON.P'
    top3all.stacked[which(top3all.stacked$TraitClean=='Creative/Imaginative'),'.id'] <- 'OPE.C'
    top3all.stacked[which(top3all.stacked$TraitClean=='Angry'),'.id'] <- 'anger'
    top3all.stacked[which(top3all.stacked$TraitClean=='Energetic'),'.id'] <- 'EXT.E'
    top3all.stacked[which(top3all.stacked$TraitClean=='Assertive'),'.id'] <- 'EXT.A'
    top3all.stacked[which(top3all.stacked$TraitClean=='Compassionate'),'.id'] <- 'AGR.C'
    top3all.stacked[which(top3all.stacked$TraitClean=='Organized'),'.id'] <- 'CON.O'
    top3all.stacked[which(top3all.stacked$TraitClean=='Trusting'),'.id'] <- 'AGR.T'
    top3all.stacked[which(top3all.stacked$TraitClean=='Intellectually Curious'),'.id'] <- 'OPE.I'
    top3all.stacked[which(top3all.stacked$TraitClean=='Responsible'),'.id'] <- 'CON.R'
    top3all.stacked[which(top3all.stacked$TraitClean=='Honest'),'.id'] <- 'MCQ.H'
    top3all.stacked[which(top3all.stacked$TraitClean=='Respectful'),'.id'] <- 'AGR.R'
    top3all.stacked[which(top3all.stacked$TraitClean=='Aesthetically Sensitive'),'.id'] <- 'OPE.A'
    top3all.stacked[which(top3all.stacked$TraitClean=='Moral'),'.id'] <- 'MCQ.GM'
    top3all.stacked[which(top3all.stacked$TraitClean=='Loyal'),'.id'] <- 'MCQ.L'
    top3all.stacked[which(top3all.stacked$TraitClean=='Pure'),'.id'] <- 'MCQ.P'
    top3all.stacked[which(top3all.stacked$TraitClean=='Fair'),'.id'] <- 'MCQ.F'
    
    top3all.stacked <- merge(top3all.stacked,moralrelevance.avg,by='.id')
    
    # merge with current levels
    top3all.stacked <- merge(top3all.stacked,currentlevels,by='.id')
    
    top3all.stacked <- setorder(top3all.stacked,M_moralrelevance)
}

addimprovementlabels <- function(df){
  df[which(df$.id=='MCQ.GM'),'Improvement'] <- 'More Moral'
  df[which(df$.id=='AGR.R'),'Improvement'] <- 'More Respectful'
  df[which(df$.id=='MCQ.F'),'Improvement'] <- 'More Fair'
  df[which(df$.id=='MCQ.H'),'Improvement'] <- 'More Honest'
  df[which(df$.id=='MCQ.L'),'Improvement'] <- 'More Loyal'
  df[which(df$.id=='AGR.C'),'Improvement'] <- 'More Compassionate'
  df[which(df$.id=='CON.R'),'Improvement'] <- 'More Responsible'
  df[which(df$.id=='MCQ.P'),'Improvement'] <- 'More Pure'
  df[which(df$.id=='AGR.T'),'Improvement'] <- 'More Trusting'
  df[which(df$.id=='CON.P'),'Improvement'] <- 'More Productive'
  df[which(df$.id=='anger'),'Improvement'] <- 'Less Angry'
  df[which(df$.id=='OPE.I'),'Improvement'] <- 'More Intellectually Curious'
  df[which(df$.id=='NEG.E'),'Improvement'] <- 'Less Emotionally Volatile'
  df[which(df$.id=='CON.O'),'Improvement'] <- 'More Organized'
  df[which(df$.id=='NEG.D'),'Improvement'] <- 'Less Depressed'
  df[which(df$.id=='EXT.E'),'Improvement'] <- 'More Energetic'
  df[which(df$.id=='OPE.C'),'Improvement'] <- 'More Creative/Imaginative'
  df[which(df$.id=='NEG.A'),'Improvement'] <- 'Less Anxious'
  df[which(df$.id=='OPE.A'),'Improvement'] <- 'More Aesthetically Sensitive'

}

create.top3.graph <- function(top3.stacked,sample){
  
  top3graph <- ggplot(top3.stacked, aes(x=Goal, y=Percent_Plot, fill=type))+
  geom_bar(stat="identity")+
  scale_fill_manual(name="",
                    values = c("#386890","#6a9bc3"),
                    guide = guide_legend(reverse=TRUE))+
  theme(legend.position='none') +
  coord_flip() +
  geom_hline(yintercept=0) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin=Percent_Plot-ci, ymax=Percent_Plot+ci), width=.1,color='#274864') +
  xlab("")+
  ylab("Percentage Who Prioritized Each Improvement \nin Top Three Change Goals") +
  theme(panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        axis.text.y =  element_text(size=14),
        axis.text.x =  element_text(size=14),
        legend.text = element_text(size=10),
        plot.margin=unit(c(1.5,.5,0,0),"cm")) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits=c(-55,55),
                     breaks = seq(-50,50,by=10),
                     labels = abs(seq(-50,50,by=10))) +
  scale_x_discrete(limits=unique(moralrelevance.avg$Improvement)) + 
  annotation_custom(label1) + 
  annotation_custom(label2) +
  annotation_custom(grobTree(textGrob(paste0("Sample ",sample), 
                                  x=0.5,  y=1.09, hjust=0.5,
                                  gp=gpar(fontsize=18, fontface="bold"))))
    
  top3graph <- ggplot_gtable(ggplot_build(top3graph))
  top3graph$layout$clip[top3graph$layout$name == "panel"] <- "off"
  
  return(top3graph)

}
```
