Figure 2, which summarizes participants’ top three most desired changes for the target, makes the targets’ personality change priorities even clearer. For these analyses, change goals that reflected a “worsening” of the trait (which fewer than 2% of participants prioritized for each trait) were not included. By focusing on participants’ desire to “improve” each trait, these analyses directly address the main question of whether people want to be *more* moral. We found that targets were less inclined to prioritize more morally-relevant improvements (Sample 1: *r*(`r self.moral.perc.1$parameter`) = `r formatrs(self.moral.perc.1$estimate)`, 95% CI [`r formatrs(self.moral.perc.1$conf.int[1])`, `r formatrs(self.moral.perc.1$conf.int[2])`], *p* = `r formatps(self.moral.perc.1$p.value)`; Sample 2: *r*(`r self.moral.perc.2$parameter`) = `r formatrs(self.moral.perc.2$estimate)`, 95% CI [`r formatrs(self.moral.perc.2$conf.int[1])`, `r formatrs(self.moral.perc.2$conf.int[2])`], *p* = `r formatps(self.moral.perc.2$p.value)`). Instead, they focused on reducing negative emotionality. For example, a large proportion of the targets reported that becoming less anxious (Sample 1: `r round(top3all.1[which(top3all.1$Goal=='Less Anxious'),'Percent_self'],2)`%; Sample 2: `r round(top3all.2[which(top3all.2$Goal=='Less Anxious'),'Percent_self'],2)`%) or less depressed (Sample 1: `r round(top3all.1[which(top3all.1$Goal=='Less Depressed'),'Percent_self'],2)`%; Sample 2: `r round(top3all.2[which(top3all.2$Goal=='Less Depressed'),'Percent_self'],2)`%) were among their top three personality change goals. These were followed by goals to become more sociable (Sample 1: `r round(top3all.1[which(top3all.1$Goal=='More Sociable'),'Percent_self'],2)`%; Sample 2: `r round(top3all.2[which(top3all.2$Goal=='More Sociable'),'Percent_self'],2)`%), less emotionally volatile (Sample 1: `r round(top3all.1[which(top3all.1$Goal=='Less Emotionally Volatile'),'Percent_self'],2)`%; Sample 2: `r round(top3all.2[which(top3all.2$Goal=='Less Emotionally Volatile'),'Percent_self'],2)`%), and more productive (Sample 1: `r round(top3all.1[which(top3all.1$Goal=='More Productive'),'Percent_self'],2)`%; Sample 2: `r round(top3all.2[which(top3all.2$Goal=='More Productive'),'Percent_self'],2)`%). Moral improvements were rarely prioritized; for example, only ~9% and ~3% of targets prioritized a goal to become more compassionate or more generally moral, respectively.

*Figure 2.* The percentage of targets or informants who prioritized each trait as one of their top 3 most desired changes. To facilitate visual comparison, the change goals are ordered from least to most morally relevant, based on the average of the moral relevance norms across the two samples (weighted equally). However, the analyses for each sample used the moral relevance norms for the respective sample. Error bars depict 95% confidence intervals.

## Do Close Others Want Us to Be More Moral?

```{r self other t-test,include=F}

overallchange.1 <- t.test(x=dat.1$tc.overall,y=dat.1$ic.overall,alternative='two.sided',paired=T)
overallchange.2 <- t.test(x=dat.2$tc.overall,y=dat.2$ic.overall,alternative='two.sided',paired=T)

compute.overallchange.g <- function(dat){
  
  overalldat.t <- dat[!is.na(dat$ic.overall),c('targetid','tc.overall')]
  overalldat.i <- dat[!is.na(dat$ic.overall),c('targetid','ic.overall')]
  
  names(overalldat.t) <- c('target','overall')
  names(overalldat.i) <- c('target','overall')
  
  overalldat.t$type <- 'Self'
  overalldat.i$type <- 'Informant'
  
  overalldat <- rbind(overalldat.t,overalldat.i)
  
  overalldat$type <- factor(overalldat$type,levels=c('Self','Informant'))
  
  overallchange.g <- dep.t.test(overall~type, block='target', data = overalldat, 
                                     sig.level=.05, digits=2)$standardized.difference
  
  return(overallchange.g)
  
}

overallchange.g.1 <- compute.overallchange.g(dat.1)
overallchange.g.2 <- compute.overallchange.g(dat.2)

#### Robustness check: Friends and parents ####

merge.friends.parents <- function(dat,informant){

  informant.friends <- informant[which(informant$it.relationship==1),
                                   c('targetid','ic.overall')] %>%
    group_by(targetid) %>% 
    summarise_all(mean,na.rm=T)

  informant.parents <- informant[which(informant$it.relationship==4),
                                     c('targetid','ic.overall')] %>%
    group_by(targetid) %>% 
    summarise_all(mean,na.rm=T)
  
  names(informant.friends)[2] <- 'ic.overall.friends'
  names(informant.parents)[2] <- 'ic.overall.parents'
  
  dat <- merge(dat,informant.friends,by='targetid',all.x=T)
  dat <- merge(dat,informant.parents,by='targetid',all.x=T)
  
  return(dat)

}

dat.1 <- merge.friends.parents(dat.1,informant.1)
dat.2 <- merge.friends.parents(dat.2,informant.2)

```

Next, we examined whether close others wanted their targets to change to a similar extent and in similar ways as the targets themselves. First, we compared targets’ and informants’ average absolute change goals across the 42 items (scores on this index ranged from 0 to 2). Paired-samples *t*-tests showed that on average, targets wanted to change themselves more (Sample 1: *M* = `r round(mean(dat.1[!is.na(dat.1$ic.overall),'tc.overall']),2)`, *SD* = `r round(sd(dat.1[!is.na(dat.1$ic.overall),'tc.overall']),2)`; Sample 2:  *M* = `r round(mean(dat.2[!is.na(dat.2$ic.overall),'tc.overall']),2)`, *SD* = `r round(sd(dat.2[!is.na(dat.2$ic.overall),'tc.overall']),2)`) than their close others wanted them to change (Sample 1: *M* = `r round(mean(dat.1$ic.overall,na.rm=T),2)`, *SD* = `r round(sd(dat.1$ic.overall,na.rm=T),2)`, *g* = `r overallchange.g.1['es.n']`, 95% CI [`r overallchange.g.1['lower.n']`, `r overallchange.g.1['upper.n']`]; Sample 2: *M* = `r round(mean(dat.2$ic.overall,na.rm=T),2)`, *SD* = `r round(sd(dat.2$ic.overall,na.rm=T),2)`, *g* = `r overallchange.g.2['es.n']`, 95% CI [`r overallchange.g.2['lower.n']`, `r overallchange.g.2['upper.n']`]). TThis pattern can be seen most clearly in Figure 1—the gray bars (depicting the percentage of targets or informants who did not want the target to change a given trait) are much larger for the informants, across all traits. In addition, the average extent to which close others wanted the target to change was descriptively very similar for both friends (Sample 1: *M* = `r round(mean(dat.1[!is.na(dat.1$ic.overall.friends),'ic.overall.friends']),2)`, *SD* = `r round(sd(dat.1[!is.na(dat.1$ic.overall.friends),'ic.overall.friends']),2)`; Sample 2: *M* = `r round(mean(dat.2[!is.na(dat.2$ic.overall.friends),'ic.overall.friends']),2)`, *SD* = `r round(sd(dat.2[!is.na(dat.2$ic.overall.friends),'ic.overall.friends']),2)`) and parents (Sample 1: *M* = `r round(mean(dat.1[!is.na(dat.1$ic.overall.parents),'ic.overall.parents']),2)`, *SD* = `r round(sd(dat.1[!is.na(dat.1$ic.overall.parents),'ic.overall.parents']),2)`; Sample 2: *M* = `r round(mean(dat.2[!is.na(dat.2$ic.overall.parents),'ic.overall.parents']),2)`, *SD* = `r round(sd(dat.2[!is.na(dat.2$ic.overall.parents),'ic.overall.parents']),2)`).

```{r priorities similarity,include=F}

top3cor.1 <- cor.test(top3all.1$Percent_self,top3all.1$Percent_other,method='pearson')
```

Although informants typically wanted to the targets to change less than the targets themselves did, they reported a similar pattern of change goals across traits, across targets, and within targets. Across traits, targets and informants showed a similar pattern of personality change priorities: the two sets of percentages (which included goals to change in the undesirable direction) correlated at *r*(`r top3cor.1$parameter`) = `r formatrs(top3cor.1$estimate)`, 95% CI [`r formatrs(top3cor.1$conf.int[1])`, `r formatrs(top3cor.1$conf.int[2])`], *p* < .001 (Sample 1) and *r*(`r top3cor.2$parameter`) = `r formatrs(top3cor.2$estimate)`, 95% CI [`r formatrs(top3cor.2$conf.int[1])`, `r formatrs(top3cor.2$conf.int[2])`], *p* < .001 (Sample 2). Mirroring the results for self-reported change goals, informants also reported lower desires to change more morally-relevant traits, *r*(`r other.testmoralrelevance.1$parameter`) = `r formatrs(other.testmoralrelevance.1$estimate)`, 95% CI [`r formatrs(other.testmoralrelevance.1$conf.int[1])`, `r formatrs(other.testmoralrelevance.1$conf.int[2])`], *p* < .001 (Sample 1) and *r*(`r other.testmoralrelevance.2$parameter`) = `r formatrs(other.testmoralrelevance.2$estimate)`, 95% CI [`r formatrs(other.testmoralrelevance.2$conf.int[1])`, `r formatrs(other.testmoralrelevance.2$conf.int[2])`], *p* < .001 (Sample 2), and were less likely to prioritize more morally-relevant improvements, *r*(`r other.testmoralrelevance.perc.1$parameter`) = `r formatrs(other.testmoralrelevance.perc.1$estimate)`, 95% CI [`r formatrs(other.testmoralrelevance.perc.1$conf.int[1])`, `r formatrs(other.testmoralrelevance.perc.1$conf.int[2])`], *p* = `r formatps(other.testmoralrelevance.perc.1$p.value)` (Sample 1) and *r*(`r other.testmoralrelevance.perc.2$parameter`) = `r formatrs(other.testmoralrelevance.perc.2$estimate)`, 95% CI [`r formatrs(other.testmoralrelevance.perc.2$conf.int[1])`, `r formatrs(other.testmoralrelevance.perc.2$conf.int[2])`], *p* = `r formatps(other.testmoralrelevance.perc.2$p.value)` (Sample 2).

We used two additional methods to examine the similarity between self- and informant-rated change goals. First, for each trait, we computed the latent correlation between self-reported change goals and informant-reported change goals (i.e., self--other agreement; see Table 2). These estimates were generally moderately positive (Sample 1: mean *r* = `r formatrs(m.agree.tc.ic.1)`; Sample 2: mean *r* = `r formatrs(m.agree.tc.ic.2)`), suggesting that targets and informants agreed to some extent on how much targets should increase or decrease on each trait. For example, if a target reported that they wanted to become much less anxious, their informants also tended to report greater goals to reduce the target’s anxiety (compared to a target who reported not wanting to reduce their anxiety).

```{r profile cors,include=F}

compute.profileout <- function(dat){
  
  profileout <- Profile.r(dat[,tc.changefacets], dat[,ic.changefacets], 
          nomiss = 1, distinct = T, alt = "two.sided")$Tests

  profileout$stat <- row.names(profileout)

  return(profileout)
  
}

profileout.1 <- compute.profileout(dat.1)
profileout.2 <- compute.profileout(dat.2)

```

Second, we computed profile correlations. Profile correlations describe the similarity between two sets of goals (i.e., across all 21 traits), as opposed to the between-person agreement for a given trait. They therefore allow us to examine the extent of similarity between a target’s idiosyncratic profile of change goals and their informants’ profile of change goals for them. However, profile correlations can be positive simply due to normativeness effects (e.g., because the average person wants to decrease on depression and increase on sociability; Furr, 2008). Because of such effects, it is theoretically possible that an “informant” who had never met a given target could report change goals that substantially overlap with that target’s goals. Therefore, we compared the average overall profile correlation to a baseline based on many “pseudo-samples” in which we randomly paired up each target’s profile of 21 change goals with the profile of 21 change goals reported by a different target’s informant(s), and recomputed the profile correlations based on 1,000 such pseudo-samples (using multicon; Sherman & Serfass, 2015). From this, we found that the mean overall *r* for both samples was `r formatrs(profileout.1[which(profileout.1$stat=='Mean'),'Overall'])` (*p* < .001). After removing normativeness effects (i.e., agreement due to the average change goal profile), there was still a small amount of distinctive profile agreement (Sample 1: *r* = `r formatrs(profileout.1[which(profileout.1$stat=='Mean'),'Distinctive'])`, *p* < .001; Sample 2: *r* = `r formatrs(profileout.2[which(profileout.2$stat=='Mean'),'Distinctive'])`, *p* < .001). That is, targets and informants showed some agreement on the profile of changes that they wanted to see in the target, over and above mere normativeness effects.

## Who Wants to Be More Moral?

Although people were generally less inclined to change more morally-relevant traits, some people showed a greater desire to change morally-relevant traits (relative to other people). Thus, we explored the correlates of these individual differences in moral change goals.

### Associations between traits and change goals.

```{r calibration effect, include=F}

#### Specify SEMs ####

MCQ.GM.mod <- 'x =~ ts.MCQ.GM1 + ts.MCQ.GM2r + ts.MCQ.GM3 + ts.MCQ.GM5
               y =~ yl*tc.MCQ.GM3 + yl*tc.MCQ.GM5
               x~~1*x
               y~~1*y'
MCQ.F.mod <- 'x =~ xl*ts.MCQ.F1 + xl*ts.MCQ.F2
              y =~ yl*tc.MCQ.F1 + yl*tc.MCQ.F4
              x~~1*x

#### Fit SEMs ####

create.maincortable <- function(dat){
  
  maincorlist <- list()

  for(i in all.main.mods){
    coefs <- parameterEstimates(sem(i,data=dat,std.lv=T))
    r <- coefs[which(coefs$lhs=='x' & coefs$rhs=='y'),c('est','pvalue','ci.lower','ci.upper')]
    maincorlist[[i]] <- r
  }
  
  names(maincorlist) <- names(all.main.mods)
  maincortable <- ldply(maincorlist)
  
  maincortable$Type <- gsub( "_.*$", "", maincortable$.id )
  maincortable$.id <- gsub( "ittc_", "", maincortable$.id )
  maincortable$.id <- gsub( "i_", "", maincortable$.id )
  maincortable$.id <- gsub( "t_", "", maincortable$.id )
  
  names(maincortable) <- c('.id','r','p','lci','uci','type')

  # Threshold any CIs that exceed |1|
  maincortable[which(maincortable$lci < -1),'lci'] <- -1
  maincortable[which(maincortable$uci > 1),'uci'] <- 1
  
  return(maincortable)
  
}

maincortable.1 <- create.maincortable(dat.1)
maincortable.2 <- create.maincortable(dat.2)

#### Forest Plot ####

create.figure3 <- function(maincortable,normtable,sample){
  
  selfplotdat <- maincortable[which(maincortable$type=='t'),]
  otherplotdat <- maincortable[which(maincortable$type=='i'),]
  selfotherdat <- maincortable[which(maincortable$type=='ittc'),]
  
  selfplotdat$Type <- 'Self'
  otherplotdat$Type <- 'Other'
  selfotherdat$Type <- 'SelfOther'
  
  normtable <- setorder(normtable,M_moralrelevance)
  
  # reorder by moral relevance rating for each sample
  selfplotdat <- selfplotdat[match(normtable$.id, selfplotdat$.id),]
  otherplotdat <- otherplotdat[match(normtable$.id, otherplotdat$.id),]
  selfotherdat <- selfotherdat[match(normtable$.id, selfotherdat$.id),]
  
  forest.table <- rbind(selfplotdat,otherplotdat,selfotherdat)
  
  forest.table <- addtraitlabels(forest.table)
  
  forest.labels <- data.frame(unique(forest.table[,c('Trait')]))
  
  forest.labels[,1] <- as.character(forest.labels[,1])
  
  xticks <- seq(-1,.3,by=.1) 
  xtlab <- c(paste0('\U2012',1),paste0('\U2012','.90'),
             paste0('\U2012','.80'),paste0('\U2012','.70'),
             paste0('\U2012','.60'),paste0('\U2012','.50'),
             paste0('\U2012','.40'),paste0('\U2012','.30'),
             paste0('\U2012','.20'),paste0('\U2012','.10'),
             paste0(0),paste0('.10'),paste0('.20'),paste0('.30'))
  attr(xticks, "labels") <- xtlab

  figure3 <- grid.grabExpr(print(forestplot(list(
    append(list(expression(bold(Trait))), 
           forest.labels[,1])), 
    legend = c("Self-Reported Traits and Change Goals", 
               "Informant-Reported Traits and Change Goals"),
    title = paste0('Sample ',sample),
    line.margin = .15,
    fn.ci_norm = c(fpDrawNormalCI,fpDrawCircleCI),
    is.summary=c(TRUE,rep(FALSE,21)),
    boxsize=.3,
    mean = cbind(c(NA,forest.table[which(forest.table$Type=='Self'), "r"]), 
                 c(NA,forest.table[which(forest.table$Type=='Other'), "r"])),
    lower = cbind(c(NA,forest.table[which(forest.table$Type=='Self'), "lci"]), 
                  c(NA,forest.table[which(forest.table$Type=='Other'), "lci"])),
    upper = cbind(c(NA,forest.table[which(forest.table$Type=='Self'), "uci"]), 
                  c(NA,forest.table[which(forest.table$Type=='Other'), "uci"])),
    vertices=T,
    col=fpColors(box=c("#6a9bc3","#386890"),
                 line=c("#6a9bc3","#386890")),
    xlab=expression(italic(r)),
    xticks=xticks,     
    clip=c(-1,.3),
    txt_gp = fpTxtGp(ticks = gpar(fontfamily = "", cex=.75),
                     xlab  = gpar(fontfamily = "", cex = 1))
  )))

  return(figure3)
  
}

#### Create clean tables ####

create.tableS10 <- function(maincortable){
  
  maincortable$est <- formatrs(maincortable$r)
  maincortable[which(maincortable$p<.05),'est'] <- paste0(maincortable[which(maincortable$p<.05),'est'],'*')
  maincortable[which(maincortable$p<.01),'est'] <- paste0(maincortable[which(maincortable$p<.01),'est'],'*')
  maincortable[which(maincortable$p<.001),'est'] <- paste0(maincortable[which(maincortable$p<.001),'est'],'*')
  
  maincortable$ci <- paste0('[',formatrs(maincortable$lci),', ',
                              formatrs(maincortable$uci),']')
  
  maincortable$p <- formatps(maincortable$p)
  
  maincortable <- addtraitlabels(maincortable)
  
  maincortable.t <- maincortable[which(maincortable$type=='t'),c('Trait','.id','est','ci','p')]
  maincortable.i <- maincortable[which(maincortable$type=='i'),c('.id','est','ci','p')]
  maincortable.ittc <- maincortable[which(maincortable$type=='ittc'),c('.id','est','ci','p')]
  
  names(maincortable.t)[3:5] <- paste0(names(maincortable.t)[3:5],'_t')
  names(maincortable.i)[2:4] <- paste0(names(maincortable.i)[2:4],'_i')
  names(maincortable.ittc)[2:4] <- paste0(names(maincortable.ittc)[2:4],'_ittc')
  
  maincortable.t <- maincortable.t[match(rev(moralrelevance.avg$.id),maincortable.t$.id),]
  maincortable.i <- maincortable.i[match(rev(moralrelevance.avg$.id),maincortable.i$.id),]
  maincortable.ittc <- maincortable.ittc[match(rev(moralrelevance.avg$.id),maincortable.ittc$.id),]
  
  tableS10 <- cbind(maincortable.t[,c('Trait','est_t','ci_t','p_t')],NA,
                   maincortable.ittc[,c('est_ittc','ci_ittc','p_ittc')],NA,
                   maincortable.i[,c('est_i','ci_i','p_i')])
  
  return(tableS10)

}
```

```{r test cor dif, include=F}
# Combine correlations from three tables into long form

combinecors <- function(maincortable,normtable.traits){
  
  comparecors.self <- maincortable[which(maincortable$type=='t'),c('.id','r')][,c('.id','r')]
  comparecors.selfother <- maincortable[which(maincortable$type=='ittc'),c('.id','r')][,c('.id','r')]
  comparecors.other <- maincortable[which(maincortable$type=='i'),c('.id','r')][,c('.id','r')]
  
  comparecors.self$type <- 'Self'
  comparecors.selfother$type <- 'SelfOther'
  comparecors.other$type <- 'Other'
  
  comparecors.long <- rbind(comparecors.self,comparecors.selfother,comparecors.other)
  
  # z-transform correlations
  comparecors.long$rz <- fisherz(comparecors.long$r)
  
  comparecors.long$type <- factor(comparecors.long$type, levels=c('Self','SelfOther','Other'))
  
  # Merge with moral relevance for each respective sample
  comparecors.long <- merge(comparecors.long,
                         normtable.traits[,c('.id','M_moralrelevance')],
                         by='.id',all.x=T)
  
  return(comparecors.long)

}

comparecors.long.1 <- combinecors(maincortable.1,normtable.traits.1)
comparecors.long.2 <- combinecors(maincortable.2,normtable.traits.2)

#### 4b: Are change goals less calibrated to current levels for more morally-relevant traits? ####

# Correlations between moral relevance and calibration of goals to current levels,
# separately for self-levels and self-goals, other-levels and self-goals,
# and other-levels and other-goals

test.moral.attenuation <- function(comparecors.long){
  
  moralrs <- data.frame(type=c('Self','SelfOther','Other'))
  
  for(i in c('Self','SelfOther','Other')){
    moralrs[which(moralrs$type==i),'r'] <- cor.test(comparecors.long[which(comparecors.long$type==i),'rz'],
                                                    comparecors.long[which(comparecors.long$type==i),
                                                                     'M_moralrelevance'])$est
    
    moralrs[which(moralrs$type==i),'p'] <- cor.test(comparecors.long[which(comparecors.long$type==i),'rz'],
                                                    comparecors.long[which(comparecors.long$type==i),
                                                                     'M_moralrelevance'])$p.value
    
     # record df and 95% CIs
    moralrs[which(moralrs$type==i),'df'] <- cor.test(comparecors.long[which(comparecors.long$type==i),'rz'],
                                                    comparecors.long[which(comparecors.long$type==i),
                                                                     'M_moralrelevance'])$parameter
    
    moralrs[which(moralrs$type==i),c('lci','uci')] <- cor.test(comparecors.long[which(comparecors.long$type==i),'rz'],
                                                    comparecors.long[which(comparecors.long$type==i),
                                                                     'M_moralrelevance'])$conf.int
    
  }
  
  return(moralrs)
  
}

moralattenuation.1 <- test.moral.attenuation(comparecors.long.1)
moralattenuation.2 <- test.moral.attenuation(comparecors.long.2)

#### 4c: Are informants more calibrated to current levels? ####

# Comparing the size of the average correlation for Self vs. Other,
# and for Self vs. SelfOther
# Expectation: Average correlation will be less negative for Self vs. Other,
# and more negative for Self vs. SelfOther

compute.self.other.t <- function(comparecors.long){
  
  self.other.t <- t.test(x=comparecors.long[which(comparecors.long$type=='Self'),'rz'],
                         y=comparecors.long[which(comparecors.long$type=='Other'),'rz'],
                         alternative='two.sided',paired=T)
  
  return(self.other.t)
  
}

compute.self.selfother.t <- function(comparecors.long){
  
  self.selfother.t <- t.test(x=comparecors.long[which(comparecors.long$type=='Self'),'rz'],
                         y=comparecors.long[which(comparecors.long$type=='SelfOther'),'rz'],
                         alternative='two.sided',paired=T)
  
  return(self.selfother.t)
  
}

self.other.t.1 <- compute.self.other.t(comparecors.long.1)
self.other.t.2 <- compute.self.other.t(comparecors.long.2)

self.selfother.t.1 <- compute.self.selfother.t(comparecors.long.1)
self.selfother.t.2 <- compute.self.selfother.t(comparecors.long.2)

#### 4d: Testing interaction hypothesis ####

# Is there a significant interaction between source (self vs. informant)
# and moral relevance in predicting how calibrated change goals are
# to current levels? 
# (i.e., is the difference between self and informant correlations larger
# for more morally-relevant goals?)

test.interaction <- function(comparecors.long,comparisontype){
 
  fit.interaction <- lmer(rz~type*M_moralrelevance + (1 |.id), 
     data=comparecors.long[which(comparecors.long$type %in% c('Self',comparisontype)),])
  
  return(fit.interaction)
  
}

interaction.self.other.1 <- test.interaction(comparecors.long.1,'Other')
interaction.self.other.2 <- test.interaction(comparecors.long.2,'Other')

# Repeat for SelfOther vs. Self comparison
# Expectation is that there will be no significant typeSelfOther:moralrelevance interaction

interaction.self.selfother.1 <- test.interaction(comparecors.long.1,'SelfOther')
interaction.self.selfother.2 <- test.interaction(comparecors.long.2,'SelfOther')

cor.test(comparecors.long.2[which(comparecors.long.2$type=='SelfOther'),'M_moralrelevance'],
         comparecors.long.2[which(comparecors.long.2$type=='SelfOther'),'rz'])

```

First, we examined whether change goals were generally calibrated to the targets’ current traits. Figure 3 (and Table S10 in the OSF repository) shows the latent correlations between current levels and change goals for each trait. Replicating the pattern observed in previous studies (e.g., Hudson & Roberts, 2014), in general, targets who reported being lower on a given trait wanted to increase more on that trait (Sample 1: mean *r* = `r formatrs(fisherz2r(mean(fisherz(maincortable.1[which(maincortable.1$type=='t'),'r']))))`; Sample 2: mean *r* = `r formatrs(fisherz2r(mean(fisherz(maincortable.2[which(maincortable.2$type=='t'),'r']))))`). However, the negative association between traits and change goals was smaller for more morally-relevant traits, as shown by a strong positive association between moral relevance scores and (Fisher *r*-to-*z* transformed) correlations between traits and change goals (Sample 1: *r*(`r moralattenuation.1[which(moralattenuation.1$type=='Self'),'df']`) = `r formatrs(moralattenuation.1[which(moralattenuation.1$type=='Self'),'r'])`, 95% CI [`r formatrs(moralattenuation.1[which(moralattenuation.1$type=='Self'),'lci'])`, `r formatrs(moralattenuation.1[which(moralattenuation.1$type=='Self'),'uci'])`], *p* = `r formatps(moralattenuation.1[which(moralattenuation.1$type=='Self'),'p'])`; Sample 2: *r*(`r moralattenuation.2[which(moralattenuation.2$type=='Self'),'df']`) = `r formatrs(moralattenuation.2[which(moralattenuation.2$type=='Self'),'r'])`, 95% CI [`r formatrs(moralattenuation.2[which(moralattenuation.2$type=='Self'),'lci'])`, `r formatrs(moralattenuation.2[which(moralattenuation.2$type=='Self'),'uci'])`], *p* = `r formatps(moralattenuation.2[which(moralattenuation.2$type=='Self'),'p'])`). That is, compared to a less morally-relevant trait, knowing someone’s current levels on a more morally-relevant trait tells you less about whether they want to increase or decrease on that trait. That is, knowing someone’s current standing on a more morally-relevant trait provides relatively little information about whether they want to increase or decrease on that trait.

*Figure 3.* Associations between current traits and change goals. Error bars depict the 95% confidence intervals. The traits are ordered from least to most morally relevant, based on the moral relevance norms for each respective sample.

We then examined the associations between informant-reported current traits and change goals. A paired-samples *t*-test showed that the negative association between traits and change goals was even stronger when both were informant-reported, compared to when both were self-reported (Sample 1: mean  $r_{informant}$ = `r formatrs(fisherz2r(mean(fisherz(maincortable.1[which(maincortable.1$type=='i'),'r']))))`, *t*(`r self.other.t.1$parameter`) = `r round(self.other.t.1$statistic,2)`, *p* < .001; Sample 2: mean $r_{informant}$ = `r formatrs(fisherz2r(mean(fisherz(maincortable.2[which(maincortable.2$type=='i'),'r']))))`, *t*(`r self.other.t.2$parameter`) = `r round(self.other.t.2$statistic,2)`, *p* < .001). In addition, there was no evidence that the association between informant-reported traits and change goals was weaker for more morally-relevant traits (Sample 1: *r*(`r moralattenuation.1[which(moralattenuation.1$type=='Other'),'df']`) = `r formatrs(moralattenuation.1[which(moralattenuation.1$type=='Other'),'r'])`, 95% CI [`r formatrs(moralattenuation.1[which(moralattenuation.1$type=='Other'),'lci'])`, `r formatrs(moralattenuation.1[which(moralattenuation.1$type=='Other'),'uci'])`], *p* = `r formatps(moralattenuation.1[which(moralattenuation.1$type=='Other'),'p'])`; Sample 2: *r*(`r moralattenuation.2[which(moralattenuation.2$type=='Other'),'df']`) = `r formatrs(moralattenuation.2[which(moralattenuation.2$type=='Other'),'r'])`, 95% CI [`r formatrs(moralattenuation.2[which(moralattenuation.2$type=='Other'),'lci'])`, `r formatrs(moralattenuation.2[which(moralattenuation.2$type=='Other'),'uci'])`], *p* = `r formatps(moralattenuation.2[which(moralattenuation.2$type=='Other'),'p'])`; but note that we had relatively low power to detect these effects). However, there was no significant interaction between moral relevance and whether traits and change goals were both self-reported (the reference category) or both informant-reported (Sample 1: *b* = `r formatbs(summary(interaction.self.other.1)$coefficients['typeOther:M_moralrelevance','Estimate'])`, 95% CI [`r formatbs(confint(interaction.self.other.1)['typeOther:M_moralrelevance',1])`, `r formatbs(confint(interaction.self.other.1)['typeOther:M_moralrelevance',2])`], *p* = `r formatps(summary(interaction.self.other.1)$coefficients['typeOther:M_moralrelevance','Pr(>|t|)'])`; Sample 2: *b* = `r formatbs(summary(interaction.self.other.2)$coefficients['typeOther:M_moralrelevance','Estimate'])`, 95% CI [`r formatbs(confint(interaction.self.other.2)['typeOther:M_moralrelevance',1])`, `r formatbs(confint(interaction.self.other.2)['typeOther:M_moralrelevance',2])`], *p* = `r formatps(summary(interaction.self.other.2)$coefficients['typeOther:M_moralrelevance','Pr(>|t|)'])`).

We conducted conceptually similar logistic regression analyses, predicting change goal priorities from current levels. This alternative approach (see Supplemental Material) showed that targets who had less desirable levels of a trait were more likely to prioritize improving that trait as one of their top three change goals, and that informants’ change goals remained relatively calibrated to their perceptions of targets’ deficits, even for morally-relevant traits.

### Associations with additional individual differences.

The above results showed that self-reported moral change goals were, at best, only weakly negatively correlated with self-reported levels on the respective traits. To find out whether moral change goals are related to other aspects of moral character and values, we used semi-partial correlations to examine the associations that each self-reported moral change goal had with a number of additional individual differences relating to moral character and values, controlling for self-reported levels on the trait in question. Two replicable and theoretically noteworthy findings were that more religious targets tended to report greater desires to increase on compassion and loyalty (controlling for self-reported compassion and loyalty, respectively), and that those who valued impartially maximizing the greater good (Kahane et al., 2018) reported greater desires to become fairer and more compassionate (controlling for self-reported fairness and compassion, respectively; see Supplemental Material and Tables S3--S4 for full details).

## Do High Trait Levels Explain Why People Don’t Want to Be More Moral?

Finally, because ratings tended to be quite high for most of the morally-relevant traits, we explored the possibility that people are less motivated to improve moral traits because they already see themselves or their close others as being relatively high on such traits (compared to less morally-relevant traits). To test this idea, we conducted supplemental within-person analyses using multi-level models. Across both samples, person-mean-centered trait levels and moral relevance independently predicted lowered change goals for both the continuous and priority-based measures, and for both self- and informant-perspectives (these analyses were not preregistered; for details, see Supplemental Material and Table S2). In other words, people were less inclined to change the traits that they saw themselves (or their targets) as being relatively higher on (compared to the target’s other traits)---but even after controlling for their perceptions of targets’ current levels, they were still less inclined to change more morally-relevant traits.

# Discussion
We examined whether people want to be more moral, and whether close others also want our moral qualities to improve. Two findings stand out. First, people were less interested in changing moral traits (e.g., honesty, fairness, compassion), compared to non-moral traits (e.g., anxiety, sociability, productiveness), in themselves and in close others. Second, targets and informants showed similar patterns of change goals, but targets wanted to change themselves to a much greater extent than did their informants.

Why don’t people particularly want to be more moral? Although self-ratings tended to be high for moral traits, ceiling effects cannot explain our main result, because our measure of change goals allowed participants to report how much they wanted to increase, decrease, or stay the same on each trait, independently of how they currently rated themselves. A more psychologically interesting possibility is that people see less room for improvement on moral traits. Because we did not measure where people think they stand relative to the extremes of each trait, our data cannot speak directly to this idea (i.e., people might not be claiming that they have the lowest or highest possible levels of each trait when they “strongly disagree” or “strongly agree” with each trait description; Blanton & Jaccard, 2006). A related possibility is that people are less motivated to improve moral traits because they already see themselves as being quite high on such traits, and therefore morally “good enough”---even if they think they *could* be morally better (see Schwitzgebel, 2019). However, even after controlling for current levels, people were still less inclined to change more morally-relevant traits, suggesting that additional psychological factors might reduce people’s desire to change morally-relevant traits.

One such possibility is that people are typically motivated to change in ways that will improve their own well-being (Hudson & Fraley, 2016). Whereas becoming less anxious has obvious personal benefits, people might believe that becoming more moral would result in few personal benefits (or even costs). Supporting this idea, targets’ and informants’ justifications for their top change goal suggested that non-moral improvements would primarily benefit the target, whereas moral improvements would primarily benefit others (see Supplemental Material). Our findings are also consistent with the idea that people are reluctant to change moral traits because they are fundamental to their identity (e.g., Riis et al., 2008).

Considering how much people value morality in others (Goodwin, 2015; Goodwin et al., 2014; Hartley et al., 2016), it is perhaps more surprising that people don’t want their close others to improve their moral qualities. Instead, like targets, informants prioritized wanting targets to become less anxious and depressed---and their open-ended justifications for these goals overwhelmingly reflected a concern for the targets’ well-being (see Supplemental Material). Similar mechanisms might explain why people don’t want themselves (described above) and others to become more moral. An additional possible explanation---specific to interpersonal change goals---is that people are less likely to become or stay close with social partners who have very different moral values in the first place (Haidt, Rosenberg, & Hom, 2003; Skitka, 2010).

Finally, targets who had less desirable levels of a given trait wanted to improve more on that trait, but this was less true for more morally-relevant traits. For example, self-perceived deficiencies on compassion and general morality were not particularly indicative of how much targets wanted to improve these traits. Interestingly, however, informants’ change goals were generally well-calibrated to their perceptions of targets’ deficits---including moral deficits. This suggests that close others might have unique insight into not only our trait levels (Quintus et al., 2017; Vazire & Carlson, 2011), but also which of our traits are most in need of improvement.

## Constraints on Generality
Our goal in asking targets to self-nominate well-acquainted informants was to understand interpersonal change goals in the context of real-world relationships. Thus, we do not expect our findings regarding interpersonal change goals to generalize beyond people who already like and are close to the targets. We would likely see a greater desire to change targets in general---and perhaps a greater desire to change moral traits specifically---if we recruited informants who disliked the targets (Leising, Erbs, & Fritz, 2010). Nor do our results speak to the moral change goals that people might have for abstract entities such as outgroups or people in general.

Does our main finding---that people are relatively unenthusiastic about moral self-improvement---generalize beyond the unique developmental context of young adulthood? For example, given that concerns for nurturing and guiding the next generation tend to peak in midlife (McAdams, de St. Aubin, & Logan, 1993), midlife adults might be more likely to prioritize moral improvements that serve these goals. We conducted another preregistered replication, which showed that relatively older adults (mean age = 45.4 years) are also less inclined to improve more morally relevant traits (see Supplemental Material, Section 8). Thus, we conclude that across the adult lifespan, people in Western cultures deprioritize moral self-improvements. Future research should investigate how other people want targets of different ages to change. For example, although parents of our young adult targets wanted them to change less than the targets themselves did, we speculate that parents might want to see greater moral development in younger children, even before children start thinking about changing their own personalities (but we have no idea what age range this might apply to).

## Conclusion
People care a lot about morality, but does that mean that they want themselves and close others to be more moral? We found that North American college students might not value moral improvements as much as non-moral improvements in themselves, and that their close others typically feel the same way. This suggests that personality change goals might be primarily motivated by the desire to improve one’s own life, rather than by more noble considerations. Still, on an uplifting note, close others generally accept us for who we are, but overwhelmingly want us to change in ways that have our best interests in mind.

# Supplemental Material

# 1. Additional Methodological Details

## Preregistration Details

Prior to collecting any data, we preregistered stopping rules for both samples and a preliminary analysis plan for Sample 1. Data collection for the two samples occurred around the same time, but we only conducted analyses for Sample 2 after preregistering the replication analysis code. Prior to uploading this preregistration, we only accessed the Sample 2 data for the purposes of extracting the informant contact information (to contact the informants that the targets nominated), and tracking how many informants had completed the study (which was handled by research assistants who were not involved in data analytic decisions).

## Successful Nominations

A nomination was “unsuccessful” if the target nominated themselves, provided a name but no email address, provided an email address of a different person than the one they nominated (and we noticed), or nominated people who informed us that they did not know the target. 

## Randomization Procedures for Change Goals Priorities

The order of the list was randomized, but due to human error in programming the survey, it was presented in a fixed order for all targets, and different fixed orders for the three (male, female, and gender-neutral) versions of the informant survey (as the randomization had been conducted separately for these surveys). For Sample 1, rank-order Spearman correlations between the order in which a trait was presented and the probability that it was selected as one of the top three priorities did not support the idea that targets and informants were systematically selecting change goals that were closer to the top of the list ($\rho$s > `r formatrs(min(testorder.est.1))`, *p*s > `r formatps(min(testorder.p.1))`). For Sample 2, this error also applied to the first 300 targets and their informants, but we subsequently corrected the issue such that the traits were presented in a randomized order for the last 200 targets and their informants.

## Procedures for Effect Size Comparisons

We computed average correlations by applying the Fisher *r*-to-*z* transformation, taking the mean of the resulting *z* statistics, then transforming the mean *z* back to a *r*. We computed average ORs by computing the mean of the unstandardized *b* coefficients, then exponentiating the mean *b*. When comparing the relative size of sets of correlations depending on whether they were based on self-reports, informant-reports, or across methods (as in Figure 3), we applied the Fisher *r*-to-*z* transformation, before conducting parametric analyses on the resulting *z* values. Similarly, when comparing the sizes of estimates from the logistic regression results or correlating these effects with other variables, we used the unstandardized *b* coefficients.

```{r restructure long,eval=T,include=F}
#### Restructure data to long ####

make.long <- function(dat,normtable.traits){

  ts.long <- melt(dat[,c('targetid',ts.currentfacets)],variable.name=".id",value.name = "current_self")
  tc.long <- melt(dat[,c('targetid',tc.changefacets)],variable.name=".id",value.name = "change_self")
  tcp.long <- melt(dat[,c('targetid',paste0('tcp.',allfacets))],variable.name=".id",value.name = "priorities_self")
  it.long <- melt(dat[,c('targetid',it.currentfacets)],variable.name=".id",value.name = "current_other")
  ic.long <- melt(dat[,c('targetid',ic.changefacets)],variable.name=".id",value.name = "change_other")
  icp.long <- melt(dat[,c('targetid',paste0('icp.',allfacets))],variable.name=".id",value.name = "priorities_other")
  
  # merge current levels & change goals
  ts.long$.id <- gsub('ts.','',ts.long$.id)
  tc.long$.id <- gsub('tc.','',tc.long$.id)
  tcp.long$.id <- gsub('tcp.','',tcp.long$.id)
  it.long$.id <- gsub('it.','',it.long$.id)
  ic.long$.id <- gsub('ic.','',ic.long$.id)
  icp.long$.id <- gsub('icp.','',icp.long$.id)
  
  long <- reduce(list(ts.long,tc.long,tcp.long,it.long,ic.long,icp.long), 
                 full_join, by = c('targetid','.id'))
  
  # merge with moral relevance ratings
  long <- merge(long,normtable.traits[,c('.id','M_moralrelevance','M_changeability')],by='.id',all=T)
  
  # reverse-score current levels for negative emotionality facets
  long[which(long$.id %in% c('NEG.A','NEG.D','NEG.E','anger')),
         c('current_self','current_other')] <- 6-long[which(long$.id %in% c('NEG.A','NEG.D','NEG.E','anger')),
         c('current_self','current_other')]
  
  # center current levels within-person
    for(i in unique(long$targetid)){
      long[which(long$targetid==i),'current_self.m'] <- mean(long[which(long$targetid==i),'current_self'],na.rm=TRUE)
      long$current_self.c <- long$current_self - long$current_self.m
      
      long[which(long$targetid==i),'current_other.m'] <- mean(long[which(long$targetid==i),'current_other'],na.rm=TRUE)
      long$current_other.c <- long$current_other - long$current_other.m
  }
    
  # convert change goals to absolute values
  long[,c('change_self','change_other')] <- abs(long[,c('change_self','change_other')])
  
  # reorder
  long <- setorder(long,targetid,M_moralrelevance)
  
  return(long)
}

datlong.1 <- make.long(dat.1,normtable.traits.1)
datlong.2 <- make.long(dat.2,normtable.traits.2)

  tc.long <- melt(dat[,c('targetid',tc.changefacets)],variable.name=".id",value.name = "change_self")
  tcp.long <- melt(dat[,c('targetid',paste0('tcp.',allfacets))],variable.name=".id",value.name = "priorities_self")
  mr.long <- melt(dat[,c('targetid',paste0('mr.',allfacets))],variable.name=".id",value.name = "moral_relevance")

  # merge current levels & change goals
  ts.long$.id <- gsub('ts.','',ts.long$.id)
  tc.long$.id <- gsub('tc.','',tc.long$.id)
  tcp.long$.id <- gsub('tcp.','',tcp.long$.id)
  mr.long$.id <- gsub('mr.','',mr.long$.id)
  
  long <- reduce(list(ts.long,tc.long,tcp.long,mr.long), 
                 full_join, by = c('targetid','.id'))
  
  # reverse-score current levels for negative emotionality facets
  long[which(long$.id %in% c('NEG.A','NEG.D','NEG.E','anger')),
         c('current_self')] <- 6-long[which(long$.id %in% c('NEG.A','NEG.D','NEG.E','anger')),
         c('current_self')]
  
  # center current levels and moral relevance within-person
    for(i in unique(long$targetid)){
      long[which(long$targetid==i),'current_self.m'] <- mean(long[which(long$targetid==i),'current_self'],na.rm=TRUE)
      long$current_self.c <- long$current_self - long$current_self.m
      
      long[which(long$targetid==i),'moral_relevance.m'] <- mean(long[which(long$targetid==i),'moral_relevance'],na.rm=TRUE)
      long$moral_relevance.c <- long$moral_relevance - long$moral_relevance.m
      
  }
    
  # convert change goals to absolute values
  long[,c('change_self')] <- abs(long[,c('change_self')])
  
  # reorder
  long <- setorder(long,targetid,moral_relevance)
  
  return(long)
}

datlong.3 <- make.long.3(dat.3)
```

# 3. Do the Effects of Moral Relevance Hold Controlling for Perceived Changeability and Current Levels?

## Perceived Changeability

Although we were primarily interested in whether change goals depended on the moral relevance of a trait, moral relevance is just one dimension that the 21 traits might differ on. Another dimension that might matter is perceived changeability. Trait raters (described in the main text) rated “the degree to which an adult can change how much of the trait they possess, if they make a deliberate effort” on a 7-point scale (1 = *Adults cannot change this trait at all*, 4 = *Adults can moderately change this trait*, 7 = *Adults can completely change this trait*). We averaged the two items for each trait, before computing the average changeability rating for each trait across all raters.

We did not find a significant association between the extent to which traits were seen as more easily changeable and the extent to which targets wanted to change them, *r*(`r self.testchangeability.1$parameter`) = `r formatrs(self.testchangeability.1$estimate)`, 95% CI [`r formatrs(self.testchangeability.1$conf.int[1])`, `r formatrs(self.testchangeability.1$conf.int[2])`], *p* = `r formatps(self.testchangeability.1$p.value)` (Sample 1) and *r*(`r self.testchangeability.2$parameter`) = `r formatrs(self.testchangeability.2$estimate)`, 95% CI [`r formatrs(self.testchangeability.2$conf.int[1])`, `r formatrs(self.testchangeability.2$conf.int[2])`], *p* = `r formatps(self.testchangeability.2$p.value)` (Sample 2). Nor were targets significantly more or less likely to prioritize goals to improve traits that were rated as being more changeable, *r*(`r self.change.perc.1$parameter`) = `r formatrs(self.change.perc.1$estimate)`, 95% CI [`r formatrs(self.change.perc.1$conf.int[1])`, `r formatrs(self.change.perc.1$conf.int[2])`], *p* = `r formatps(self.change.perc.1$p.value)` (Sample 1) and *r*(`r self.change.perc.2$parameter`) = `r formatrs(self.change.perc.2$estimate)`, 95% CI [`r formatrs(self.change.perc.2$conf.int[1])`, `r formatrs(self.change.perc.2$conf.int[2])`], *p* = `r formatps(self.change.perc.2$p.value)` (Sample 2). Finally, mirroring the results observed for targets, we did not find a significant association between the perceived changeability of a trait and the extent to which informants wanted to change them, *r*(`r other.testchangeability.1$parameter`) = `r formatrs(other.testchangeability.1$estimate)`, 95% CI [`r formatrs(other.testchangeability.1$conf.int[1])`, `r formatrs(other.testchangeability.1$conf.int[2])`], *p* = `r formatps(other.testchangeability.1$p.value)` (Sample 1) and *r*(`r other.testchangeability.2$parameter`) = `r formatrs(other.testchangeability.2$estimate)`, 95% CI [`r formatrs(other.testchangeability.2$conf.int[1])`, `r formatrs(other.testchangeability.2$conf.int[2])`], *p* = `r formatps(other.testchangeability.2$p.value)` (Sample 2), or the extent to which informants prioritized goals to improve these traits, *r*(`r other.change.perc.1$parameter`) = `r formatrs(other.change.perc.1$estimate)`, 95% CI [`r formatrs(other.change.perc.1$conf.int[1])`, `r formatrs(other.change.perc.1$conf.int[2])`], *p* = `r formatps(other.change.perc.1$p.value)` (Sample 1) and *r*(`r other.change.perc.2$parameter`) = `r formatrs(other.change.perc.2$estimate)`, 95% CI [`r formatrs(other.change.perc.2$conf.int[1])`, `r formatrs(other.change.perc.2$conf.int[2])`], *p* = `r formatps(other.change.perc.2$p.value)` (Sample 2). However, an important caveat is that with 21 traits, we only had 80% power to detect correlations ≥ |.57|.


```{r control changeability,include=F}

#### Fit MLMs ####

fit.mlms.change.moralrel <- function(datlong){
  mod.tc <- lmerTest::lmer(change_self~M_changeability+M_moralrelevance+
               (1 + M_changeability+M_moralrelevance|targetid),data=datlong,
               control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"))

  mod.ic <- lmerTest::lmer(change_other~M_changeability+M_moralrelevance+
                 (1 + M_changeability+M_moralrelevance|targetid),data=datlong,
                 control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"))
  
  mod.tcp <- glmer(priorities_self ~ M_changeability + M_moralrelevance + 
            (0 + M_changeability + M_moralrelevance | targetid),
            family=binomial, data=datlong)
  
  mod.icp <- glmer(priorities_other ~ M_changeability + M_moralrelevance + 
            (0 + M_changeability + M_moralrelevance | targetid),
            family=binomial, data=datlong)
  
  mlm.list <- list(mod.tc,mod.ic,mod.tcp,mod.icp)
  
  # Get coefficients and p values
  
  # Extract coefficients from ind models
  mlm.coefs <- lapply(mlm.list,function(x){
    x <- data.frame(summary(x)$coefficients)
    names(x) <- gsub('r...t..','',names(x))
    names(x) <- gsub('r...z..','',names(x))
    x <- x[!row.names(x) %in% c('(Intercept)'),c('Estimate','P')]
    names(x)[2] <- 'pval'
    x$predictor <- row.names(x)
    x
  })
  
  names(mlm.coefs) <- c('mod.tc','mod.ic','mod.tcp','mod.icp')
  mlm.coefs <- ldply(mlm.coefs)
  
  # Get 95% CIs
  mlm.cis <- lapply(mlm.list,function(x){
    confint(x,method='Wald')
  })
  
  mlm.cis <- lapply(mlm.cis,function(x){
    x <- data.frame(x[which(row.names(x) %in% c('M_changeability','M_moralrelevance')),])
    x$predictor <- row.names(x)
    x
  })
  
  names(mlm.cis) <- c('mod.tc','mod.ic','mod.tcp','mod.icp')
  mlm.cis <- ldply(mlm.cis)
  names(mlm.cis)[2:3] <- c('lci','uci')
  
  # Match 95% CIs with point estimates
  mlm.coefs <- merge(mlm.coefs,mlm.cis,by=c('.id','predictor'))
  
  return(mlm.coefs)
  
}

mlm.coefs.change.moralrel.1 <- fit.mlms.change.moralrel(datlong.1)
mlm.coefs.change.moralrel.2 <- fit.mlms.change.moralrel(datlong.2)

#### Standardize coefficients and clean up table ####

get.wpsd <- function(null){
  # This function extracts within-person SD from a fitted null model
  varcorr <- data.frame(lme4::VarCorr(null))
  wpvar <- varcorr[which(varcorr$grp=='Residual'),'vcov']
  wpsd <- sqrt(wpvar)
  return(wpsd)
}

create.wpsd.table <- function(datlong,normtable.traits){
  # This function creates a table with all of the SDs needed
  # for standardized estimates
  
  # Fit null models
  null.list <- list()
  null.list <- lapply(c('current_self','change_self',
                        'current_other','change_other'), 
                      function(var){
    form = paste(var,"~(1|targetid)")
    lme4::lmer(form, data=datlong)
  })
  
  null.order <- c('current_self','change_self',
                        'current_other','change_other')
  
  wpsd.list <- lapply(null.list,get.wpsd)
  
  names(wpsd.list) <- null.order
  
  # convert list to table
  wpsd.table <- ldply(wpsd.list)
  
  # add SD for moral relevance
  wpsd.table <- rbind(wpsd.table,
                        c('M_moralrelevance',
                          sd(normtable.traits$M_moralrelevance)),
                       c('M_changeability',
                          sd(normtable.traits$M_changeability)))
  
  names(wpsd.table)[1] <- 'predictor'
  names(wpsd.table)[2] <- 'SD_WP'
  
  return(wpsd.table)

}

wpsd.1 <- create.wpsd.table(datlong.1,normtable.traits.1)
wpsd.2 <- create.wpsd.table(datlong.2,normtable.traits.2)

create.cleancoefs.change.moralrel <- function(mlm.coefs,wpsd){
  mlm.coefs$predictor <- gsub('.c','',mlm.coefs$predictor,fixed=T)
  
  mlm.coefs[which(mlm.coefs$predictor=='M_changeability'),'SD_WP'] <- wpsd[which(wpsd$predictor=='M_changeability'),'SD_WP']
  mlm.coefs[which(mlm.coefs$predictor=='M_moralrelevance'),'SD_WP'] <- wpsd[which(wpsd$predictor=='M_moralrelevance'),'SD_WP']
  
  mlm.coefs[which(mlm.coefs$.id=='mod.tc'),'SD_WP_y'] <- wpsd[which(wpsd$predictor=='change_self'),'SD_WP']
  mlm.coefs[which(mlm.coefs$.id=='mod.ic'),'SD_WP_y'] <- wpsd[which(wpsd$predictor=='change_other'),'SD_WP']
  
  mlm.coefs[,c('SD_WP','SD_WP_y')] <- sapply(mlm.coefs[,c('SD_WP','SD_WP_y')],as.numeric)
   
  mlm.coefs[which(mlm.coefs$.id %in% c('mod.tc','mod.ic')),'type'] <- 'continuous'
  mlm.coefs[which(mlm.coefs$.id %in% c('mod.tcp','mod.icp')),'type'] <- 'priorities'
  
  # standardize beta coefficients for continuous change goals against
  # within-person SD of both X & Y
  mlm.coefs[which(mlm.coefs$type=='continuous'),
            c('est_std','lci_std','uci_std')] <- sapply(
              mlm.coefs[which(mlm.coefs$type=='continuous'),c('Estimate','lci','uci')],
            function(x){
              x*mlm.coefs[which(mlm.coefs$type=='continuous'),'SD_WP']/
                mlm.coefs[which(mlm.coefs$type=='continuous'),'SD_WP_y']})
    
  # standardize beta coefficients for priorities against within-person SD of X
  mlm.coefs[which(mlm.coefs$type=='priorities'),
            c('est_std','lci_std','uci_std')] <- sapply(
              mlm.coefs[which(mlm.coefs$type=='priorities'),c('Estimate','lci','uci')],
            function(x){
              x*mlm.coefs[which(mlm.coefs$type=='priorities'),'SD_WP']})
    
  # exponentiate standardized coefficients
  
  mlm.coefs[,c('est_clean','lci_clean','uci_clean')] <- mlm.coefs[,c('est_std','lci_std','uci_std')]
  
  mlm.coefs[which(mlm.coefs$type=='priorities'),
            c('est_clean','lci_clean','uci_clean')] <- sapply(
  mlm.coefs[which(mlm.coefs$type=='priorities'),
            c('est_std','lci_std','uci_std')],exp)
  
  # tidy up for results table
  mlm.coefs[,c('est_clean','lci_clean','uci_clean')] <- sapply(mlm.coefs[,c('est_clean','lci_clean','uci_clean')],function(x){round(x,2)})
  
  mlm.coefs[which(mlm.coefs$pval<.05),'est_clean'] <- paste0(mlm.coefs[which(mlm.coefs$pval<.05),'est_clean'],'*')
  mlm.coefs[which(mlm.coefs$pval<.01),'est_clean'] <- paste0(mlm.coefs[which(mlm.coefs$pval<.01),'est_clean'],'*')
  mlm.coefs[which(mlm.coefs$pval<.001),'est_clean'] <- paste0(mlm.coefs[which(mlm.coefs$pval<.001),'est_clean'],'*')
  
  mlm.coefs$est_clean <- paste0(mlm.coefs$est_clean,' [',
                                mlm.coefs$lci_clean,', ',
                                mlm.coefs$uci_clean,']')
  
  mlm.coefs[which(mlm.coefs$.id %in% c('mod.tc','mod.tcp')),'perspective'] <- 'Self'
  mlm.coefs[which(mlm.coefs$.id %in% c('mod.ic','mod.icp')),'perspective'] <- 'Informant'
 
  mlm.coefs.current <- mlm.coefs[which(mlm.coefs$predictor=='M_changeability'),
                                 c('type','perspective','est_clean')]
  
  names(mlm.coefs.current)[3] <- 'Changeability'
  
  mlm.coefs.moral <- mlm.coefs[which(mlm.coefs$predictor=='M_moralrelevance'),
                                 c('type','perspective','est_clean')]
  
  names(mlm.coefs.moral)[3] <- 'Moral Relevance'
  
  clean.coefs <- merge(mlm.coefs.current,mlm.coefs.moral,by=c('type','perspective'))
  
  clean.coefs[which(clean.coefs$type=='continuous'),'order1'] <- 1
  clean.coefs[which(clean.coefs$type=='priorities'),'order1'] <- 2
  clean.coefs[which(clean.coefs$perspective=='Self'),'order2'] <- 1
  clean.coefs[which(clean.coefs$perspective=='Informant'),'order2'] <- 2
  
  clean.coefs <- setorder(clean.coefs,order1,order2)
  clean.coefs <- clean.coefs[,c('perspective','Changeability','Moral Relevance')]
  
  clean.coefs <- rbind(c('Continuous',NA,NA),
                       clean.coefs[1:2,],
                       c('Priorities (OR)',NA,NA),
                       clean.coefs[3:4,])
  return(clean.coefs)
}

clean.coefs.change.moralrel.1 <- create.cleancoefs.change.moralrel(mlm.coefs.change.moralrel.1,wpsd.1)
clean.coefs.change.moralrel.2 <- create.cleancoefs.change.moralrel(mlm.coefs.change.moralrel.2,wpsd.2)

clean.coefs.change.moralrel <- cbind(clean.coefs.change.moralrel.1,NA,clean.coefs.change.moralrel.2[,2:3])

```

To gain greater precision in testing this question, we conducted exploratory (i.e., non-preregistered) analyses using a multi-level modeling approach (implemented via *lme4* and *lmerTest*; Bates, Mächler, Bolker, & Walker, 2015; Kuznetsova, Brockhoff, & Christensen, 2017). In each of these models, we predicted either continuous absolute change goals or priorities from perceived changeability and moral relevance (as simultaneous predictors), with 21 observations (for each of the 21 traits) nested within each participant. We conducted analyses separately for self- and informant-reported change goals. All models included random slopes for both perceived changeability and moral relevance, which allows each participant to have a different association between change goals and both perceived changeability and moral relevance. The models for the continuous change goals also had random intercepts, which allows each participant to have a different level of overall desired change (recall that this analysis was conducted on absolute scores that captured desired changes in either direction). The multi-level logistic regression models for predicting priorities only had a fixed intercept, because all participants had to select three priorities (which means that there was only within-persons variability, and no between-persons variability, on these outcome variables).

Across all models, the results showed that, controlling for perceived changeability, moral relevance continued to predict lowered change goals across both samples, for both self- and informant-perspectives, and for predicting continuous change goals and priorities (see Table S2). These results also provided some evidence that people were more inclined to change traits that independent raters had judged as being more changeable, though these effects were smaller and less consistent than the effects of moral relevance.

```{r control current levels,include=F}
                                 c('type','perspective','est_clean')]
  
  names(mlm.coefs.current)[3] <- 'Current Levels'
  
  mlm.coefs.moral <- mlm.coefs[which(mlm.coefs$predictor=='M_moralrelevance'),
                                 c('type','perspective','est_clean')]
  
  names(mlm.coefs.moral)[3] <- 'Moral Relevance'
  
  clean.coefs <- merge(mlm.coefs.current,mlm.coefs.moral,by=c('type','perspective'))
  
  clean.coefs[which(clean.coefs$type=='continuous'),'order1'] <- 1
  clean.coefs[which(clean.coefs$type=='priorities'),'order1'] <- 2
  clean.coefs[which(clean.coefs$perspective=='Self'),'order2'] <- 1
  clean.coefs[which(clean.coefs$perspective=='Informant'),'order2'] <- 2
  
  clean.coefs <- setorder(clean.coefs,order1,order2)
  clean.coefs <- clean.coefs[,c('perspective','Current Levels','Moral Relevance')]
  
  clean.coefs <- rbind(c('Continuous',NA,NA),
                       clean.coefs[1:2,],
                       c('Priorities (OR)',NA,NA),
                       clean.coefs[3:4,])
  return(clean.coefs)
}

clean.coefs.1 <- create.cleancoefs(mlm.coefs.1,wpsd.1)
clean.coefs.2 <- create.cleancoefs(mlm.coefs.2,wpsd.2)

clean.coefs <- cbind(clean.coefs.1,NA,clean.coefs.2[,2:3])

names.clean.coefs <- names(clean.coefs)
names(clean.coefs) <- NA

clean.coefs <- rbind(names.clean.coefs,clean.coefs)

names.clean.coefs.change.moralrel <- names(clean.coefs.change.moralrel)
names(clean.coefs.change.moralrel) <- NA

clean.coefs.change.moralrel <- rbind(names.clean.coefs.change.moralrel,clean.coefs.change.moralrel)

tableS2 <- rbind(clean.coefs.change.moralrel,clean.coefs)

write.csv(tableS2,'./Tables/tableS2.csv',row.names=F,na='')

```

Because ratings of most of the morally-relevant traits tended to be quite high (on a 5-point scale anchored by *strongly disagree* and *strongly agree*), one remaining question is how much perceptions of current trait levels might play a role in explaining why people are less inclined to change moral traits. One possibility is that people believe that there is less room for improvement on moral traits. Because “agreeing strongly” with a given item (e.g., “Is compassionate, has a soft heart”) is not the same as believing that you have the maximum possible levels of that trait, we do not have the data to test this idea. Such a test would require more direct measures of people’s perceptions of room for improvement (e.g., measuring current levels using a response scale that ranges from 0 = *lowest possible levels* to 10 = *highest possible levels*).

A second possibility is that people are simply less motivated to improve moral traits because they already see themselves as being relatively high on such traits (compared to less morally-relevant traits). This seems to be an inherently within-persons question, in contrast to the between-persons correlations we reported in the main text. Between-persons correlations between current levels and change goals for each trait ask whether people who are higher on a trait (relative to other people) want to change more on that trait (relative to other people). The within-persons approach answers a complementary question---how trait levels and change goals are related at the within-person level (i.e., do people want to change less on traits that they see themselves as being relatively high on, compared to their other traits?). We also wanted to test whether people were still less inclined to change more morally-relevant traits, controlling for their perceptions of their current levels (using this within-persons approach).

We explored these questions using the multi-level modeling approach described above (again, these analyses were not preregistered). The only difference was that we replaced perceived changeability with current levels as a predictor; thus, we predicted continuous absolute change goals or priorities from current levels and moral relevance (entered as simultaneous predictors). We reverse-scored current levels for the negative emotionality facets (anxiety, depression, emotionality, and anger), such that higher scores on all traits represent more desirable levels. Then, we centered current level scores around each person’s mean, to ensure that all effects were at the within-person level.

Across both samples, the results showed that current levels and moral relevance independently predicted lowered change goals for both the continuous and priority-based measures, and for both self- and informant-perspectives (see Table S2). For example, in Sample 1, each 1 SD increase in self-reported current levels and moral relevance (rated by independent raters) predicted an average --0.34 SD and --0.19 SD decrease in absolute change goals, respectively. In Sample 1, each 1 SD increase in self-reported current levels and moral relevance also predicted an average decrease of 2.70 and 1.92, respectively, in the odds of prioritizing an improvement on a given trait (these lowered odds were calculating by taking the inverse of 0.37 and 0.52, reported in Table S2). In other words, people were less inclined to change the traits that they saw themselves as having relatively more desirable levels of (compared with their other traits)---but even after controlling for targets’ perceptions of their current levels, they were still less inclined to change more morally-relevant traits (and the same was true from the perspective of informants).

# 4. Associations Between Informant-Reported Current Levels and Self-Reported Change Goals

Results for the associations between informant-reported current levels and self-reported change goals are shown in Table S10 in the OSF repository. The calibration to current traits was weaker (compared to the self-report-only correlations), but still generally held (Sample 1: mean *r* = `r formatrs(fisherz2r(mean(fisherz(maincortable.1[which(maincortable.1$type=='ittc'),'r']))))`; Sample 2: mean *r* = `r formatrs(fisherz2r(mean(fisherz(maincortable.2[which(maincortable.2$type=='ittc'),'r']))))`). We also observed a substantial attenuation-by-morality effect in Sample 1 (*r*(`r moralattenuation.1[which(moralattenuation.1$type=='SelfOther'),'df']`) = `r formatrs(moralattenuation.1[which(moralattenuation.1$type=='SelfOther'),'r'])`, 95% CI [`r formatrs(moralattenuation.1[which(moralattenuation.1$type=='SelfOther'),'lci'])`, `r formatrs(moralattenuation.1[which(moralattenuation.1$type=='SelfOther'),'uci'])`], *p* < .001), though the 95% CI just captured zero in Sample 2 (*r*(`r moralattenuation.2[which(moralattenuation.2$type=='SelfOther'),'df']`) = `r formatrs(moralattenuation.2[which(moralattenuation.2$type=='SelfOther'),'r'])`, 95% CI [`r formatrs(moralattenuation.2[which(moralattenuation.2$type=='SelfOther'),'lci'])`, `r formatrs(moralattenuation.2[which(moralattenuation.2$type=='SelfOther'),'uci'])`], *p* = `r formatps(moralattenuation.2[which(moralattenuation.2$type=='SelfOther'),'p'])`). To examine whether the size of the moral attenuation effect depended on whether current levels and change goals were both self-reported (vs.when only change goals were self-reported), we fit a linear mixed-effects model (with random intercepts for each trait) that regressed the Fisher *r*-to-*z* transformed correlation between current levels and change goals for each trait onto the moral relevance of each trait, the method (0 = self-reported current levels and change goals, 1 = informant-reported current levels and self-reported change goals), and the interaction between moral relevance and method. A non-significant interaction in Sample 1 suggested that the size of the moral attenuation effect did not differ significantly when current levels and change goals were both self-reported, compared to when only change goals were self-reported, *b* = `r formatbs(summary(interaction.self.selfother.1)$coefficients['typeSelfOther:M_moralrelevance','Estimate'])`, 95% CI [`r formatbs(confint(interaction.self.selfother.1)['typeSelfOther:M_moralrelevance',1])`, `r formatbs(confint(interaction.self.selfother.1)['typeSelfOther:M_moralrelevance',2])`], *p* = `r formatps(summary(interaction.self.selfother.1)$coefficients['typeSelfOther:M_moralrelevance','Pr(>|t|)'])`; however, this interaction was significant in Sample 2, suggesting that there was less of a moral attenuation effect when current levels were reported by informants,  *b* = `r formatbs(summary(interaction.self.selfother.2)$coefficients['typeSelfOther:M_moralrelevance','Estimate'])`, 95% CI [`r formatbs(confint(interaction.self.selfother.2)['typeSelfOther:M_moralrelevance',1])`, `r formatbs(confint(interaction.self.selfother.2)['typeSelfOther:M_moralrelevance',2])`], *p* = `r formatps(summary(interaction.self.selfother.2)$coefficients['typeSelfOther:M_moralrelevance','Pr(>|t|)'])`.

# 5. Predicting Change Goal Priorities from Undesirable Current Levels

```{r create figure s1, include=F}
mplusout.1 <- readModels(paste0(getwd(),'/mplus-sample1'))
mplusout.2 <- readModels(paste0(getwd(),'/mplus-sample2'))

clean.mplus.out <- function(mplusout){
  
    mplusout.coefs <- lapply(mplusout,function(x){
    x <- x$parameters$unstandardized
    x <- x[-which(x$paramHeader %in% c('X.BY','Means','Intercepts','Thresholds',
                                  'Variances','Residual.Variances')),]
    x
  })
  
  mplusout.cis <- lapply(mplusout,function(x){
    x <- x$parameters$ci.unstandardized
    x <- x[-which(x$paramHeader %in% c('X.BY','Means','Intercepts','Thresholds',
                                  'Variances','Residual.Variances')),]
    x
  })
  
  mplusout.coefs <- ldply(mplusout.coefs)
  mplusout.cis <- ldply(mplusout.cis)
  
  mplusout.all <- merge(mplusout.coefs[,c('.id','est','pval')],
                        mplusout.cis[,c('.id','low2.5','up2.5')],by='.id')
  
  #### Tidy up table ####
  
  # extract type
  mplusout.all$typeid <- substr(mplusout.all$.id,1,6)
  mplusout.all[which(mplusout.all$typeid=='icp_it'),'Type'] <- 'Other'
  mplusout.all[which(mplusout.all$typeid=='tcp_ts'),'Type'] <- 'Self'
  mplusout.all[which(mplusout.all$typeid=='tcp_it'),'Type'] <- 'SelfOther'
  
  # extract trait
  mplusout.all$.id <- substring(mplusout.all$.id,8)
  mplusout.all$.id <- gsub('.out','',mplusout.all$.id)
  mplusout.all$.id <- gsub('_','.',mplusout.all$.id)
  mplusout.all[which(mplusout.all$.id=='F'),'.id'] <- 'MCQ.F'
  mplusout.all[which(mplusout.all$.id=='H'),'.id'] <- 'MCQ.H'
  mplusout.all[which(mplusout.all$.id=='L'),'.id'] <- 'MCQ.L'
  mplusout.all[which(mplusout.all$.id=='GM'),'.id'] <- 'MCQ.GM'
  mplusout.all[which(mplusout.all$.id=='P'),'.id'] <- 'MCQ.P'
  
  # reverse sign for non-neuroticism traits
  
  noreverse <- c('NEG.A','NEG.D','NEG.E','anger')
  
  mplusout.all$est.r <- -1*mplusout.all$est
  mplusout.all$low2.5r <- -1*mplusout.all$up2.5
  mplusout.all$up2.5r <- -1*mplusout.all$low2.5
  
  mplusout.all[which(mplusout.all$.id %in% noreverse),
               c('est.r','low2.5r','up2.5r')] <- mplusout.all[which(mplusout.all$.id %in% noreverse),
               c('est','low2.5','up2.5')]
  
  # exponeniate for odds ratios
  mplusout.all[,c('OR','OR_lci','OR_uci')] <- exp(mplusout.all[,c('est.r','low2.5r','up2.5r')])
  
  mplusout.all[,!names(mplusout.all) %in% 
                 c('.id','typeid','Type')] <- sapply(mplusout.all[,!names(mplusout.all) %in%
                                                                    c('.id','typeid','Type')],as.numeric)

  return(mplusout.all)

}

create.logregplot <- function(mplusout.all,normtable,sample){
  
  logregdat.self <- mplusout.all[which(mplusout.all$Type=='Self'),c('.id','OR','OR_lci','OR_uci')]
  logregdat.selfother <- mplusout.all[which(mplusout.all$Type=='SelfOther'),c('.id','OR','OR_lci','OR_uci')]
  logregdat.other <- mplusout.all[which(mplusout.all$Type=='Other'),c('.id','OR','OR_lci','OR_uci')]
  
  logregdat.self$Type <- 'Self'
  logregdat.selfother$Type <- 'SelfOther'
  logregdat.other$Type <- 'Other'
  
  normtable <- setorder(normtable,M_moralrelevance)
  
  # reorder by moral relevance rating for each sample
  logregdat.self <- logregdat.self[match(normtable$.id, logregdat.self$.id),]
  logregdat.selfother <- logregdat.selfother[match(normtable$.id, logregdat.selfother$.id),]
  logregdat.other <- logregdat.other[match(normtable$.id, logregdat.other$.id),]
  
  forest.table.logreg <- rbind(logregdat.self,logregdat.other,logregdat.selfother)
  
  forest.table.logreg <- addtraitlabels(forest.table.logreg)
  
  forest.labels.logreg <- data.frame(unique(forest.table.logreg[,c('Trait')]))
  
  forest.labels.logreg[,1] <- as.character(forest.labels.logreg[,1])
  
  forest.logreg <- grid.grabExpr(print(forestplot(list(
    append(list(expression(bold(Trait))), 
           forest.labels.logreg[,1])), 
    legend = c("Self-Reported Traits and Change Priorities", "Informant-Reported Traits and Change Priorities"),
    line.margin = .15,
    fn.ci_norm = c(fpDrawNormalCI,fpDrawCircleCI),
    is.summary=c(TRUE,rep(FALSE,21)),
    boxsize=.2,
    mean = cbind(c(NA,forest.table.logreg[which(forest.table.logreg$Type=='Self'), "OR"]), 
                 c(NA,forest.table.logreg[which(forest.table.logreg$Type=='Other'), "OR"])),
    lower = cbind(c(NA,forest.table.logreg[which(forest.table.logreg$Type=='Self'), "OR_lci"]), 
                  c(NA,forest.table.logreg[which(forest.table.logreg$Type=='Other'), "OR_lci"])),
    upper = cbind(c(NA,forest.table.logreg[which(forest.table.logreg$Type=='Self'), "OR_uci"]), 
                  c(NA,forest.table.logreg[which(forest.table.logreg$Type=='Other'), "OR_uci"])),
    vertices=T,
    col=fpColors(box=c("#6a9bc3","#386890"),
                 line=c("#6a9bc3","#386890")),
    xlab=('Odds Ratio'),
    xticks=c(0.12,0.25,0.50,1,2,4,8),      
    xlog=TRUE,
    clip =c(.12, 8),
    txt_gp = fpTxtGp(ticks = gpar(fontfamily = "", cex=.75),
                     xlab  = gpar(fontfamily = "", cex = 1)), 
    title = paste0('Sample ',sample)
    )))

  return(forest.logreg)
  
}
```

```{r moral relevance attenuation, include=F}
#### 4b: Are change goals less calibrated to current levels for more morally-relevant traits? ####

combine.logreg <- function(mplusout.all,normtable.traits){
  
  # combine estimates with norms
  compare.logreg <- merge(normtable.traits[,c('.id','Trait','M_moralrelevance')],
                              mplusout.all[which(mplusout.all$Type=='Self'),c('.id','est.r')],
                              by='.id')
  
  names(compare.logreg)[4] <- 'b_self'
  
  compare.logreg <- merge(compare.logreg,mplusout.all[which(mplusout.all$Type=='SelfOther'),
                                                                            c('.id','est.r')],
                                     by='.id')
  
  names(compare.logreg)[5] <- 'b_selfother'
  
  compare.logreg <- merge(compare.logreg,mplusout.all[which(mplusout.all$Type=='Other'),
                                                                            c('.id','est.r')],
                                     by='.id')
  
  names(compare.logreg)[6] <- 'b_other'

  return(compare.logreg)
  
}

compare.logreg.1 <- combine.logreg(mplusout.all.1,normtable.traits.1)
compare.logreg.2 <- combine.logreg(mplusout.all.2,normtable.traits.2)

test.moral.attenuation.logreg <- function(compare.logreg){
  
  moralbs <- data.frame(type=c('self','selfother','other'))
  
  for(i in c('self','selfother','other')){
    moralbs[which(moralbs$type==i),'r'] <- cor.test(compare.logreg[,paste0('b_',i)],
                                                    compare.logreg[,'M_moralrelevance'])$est
    
    moralbs[which(moralbs$type==i),'p'] <- cor.test(compare.logreg[,paste0('b_',i)],
                                                    compare.logreg[,'M_moralrelevance'])$p.value  
    
    moralbs[which(moralbs$type==i),'df'] <- cor.test(compare.logreg[,paste0('b_',i)],
                                                    compare.logreg[,'M_moralrelevance'])$parameter
    
    moralbs[which(moralbs$type==i),'lci'] <- cor.test(compare.logreg[,paste0('b_',i)],
                                                    compare.logreg[,'M_moralrelevance'])$conf.int[1]
    
    moralbs[which(moralbs$type==i),'uci'] <- cor.test(compare.logreg[,paste0('b_',i)],
                                                    compare.logreg[,'M_moralrelevance'])$conf.int[2]
  }
  
  return(moralbs)
  
}

moralattenuation.logreg.1 <- test.moral.attenuation.logreg(compare.logreg.1)
moralattenuation.logreg.2 <- test.moral.attenuation.logreg(compare.logreg.2)

  comparebs.long$type <- factor(comparebs.long$type, levels=c('Self','SelfOther','Other'))

  return(comparebs.long)

}
```
