To complement the correlational analyses, we predicted change goal priorities from undesirable current levels (modeled as latent variables) using logistic regression models implemented in Mplus Version 8.3 (Muthén & Muthén, 1998–2017). We reversed the coefficients for all facets apart from negative emotionality; thus, the resulting odds ratios (ORs) reflect the extent to which each 1 SD difference towards the undesirable direction of a trait predicted a goal to prioritize improving that trait.

Figure S1 shows that in general, targets who self-reported less desirable levels of a trait were more likely to prioritize a goal to improve that trait (as one of their top three goals; Sample 1: mean OR = `r round(exp(mean(compare.logreg.1$b_self)),2)`; Sample 2: mean OR = `r round(exp(mean(compare.logreg.2$b_self)),2)`). These odds ratios trended towards being smaller for more morally-relevant traits in Sample 1 (*r*(`r moralattenuation.logreg.1[which(moralattenuation.logreg.1$type=='self'),'df']`) = `r formatrs(moralattenuation.logreg.1[which(moralattenuation.logreg.1$type=='self'),'r'])`, 95% CI [`r formatrs(moralattenuation.logreg.1[which(moralattenuation.logreg.1$type=='self'),'lci'])`, `r formatrs(moralattenuation.logreg.1[which(moralattenuation.logreg.1$type=='self'),'uci'])`], *p* = `r formatps(moralattenuation.logreg.1[which(moralattenuation.logreg.1$type=='self'),'p'])`), but not in Sample 2 (*r*(`r moralattenuation.logreg.2[which(moralattenuation.logreg.2$type=='self'),'df']`) = `r formatrs(moralattenuation.logreg.2[which(moralattenuation.logreg.2$type=='self'),'r'])`, 95% CI [`r formatrs(moralattenuation.logreg.2[which(moralattenuation.logreg.2$type=='self'),'lci'])`, `r formatrs(moralattenuation.logreg.2[which(moralattenuation.logreg.2$type=='self'),'uci'])`], *p* = `r formatps(moralattenuation.logreg.2[which(moralattenuation.logreg.2$type=='self'),'p'])`).

Next, we predicted self-reported priorities from informant-reported current levels. These effects were smaller than for the self-report-only effects (Sample 1: mean OR = `r round(exp(mean(compare.logreg.1$b_selfother)),2)`, *t*(`r self.selfother.logreg.t.1$parameter`) = `r round(self.selfother.logreg.t.1$statistic,2)`, *p* < .001; Sample 2: mean OR = `r round(exp(mean(compare.logreg.2$b_selfother)),2)`, *t*(`r self.selfother.logreg.t.2$parameter`) = `r round(self.selfother.logreg.t.2$statistic,2)`, *p* < .001). These effects were also smaller for more morally-relevant traits in Sample 1 (*r*(`r moralattenuation.logreg.1[which(moralattenuation.logreg.1$type=='selfother'),'df']`) = `r formatrs(moralattenuation.logreg.1[which(moralattenuation.logreg.1$type=='selfother'),'r'])`, 95% CI [`r formatrs(moralattenuation.logreg.1[which(moralattenuation.logreg.1$type=='selfother'),'lci'])`, `r formatrs(moralattenuation.logreg.1[which(moralattenuation.logreg.1$type=='selfother'),'uci'])`], *p* = `r formatps(moralattenuation.logreg.1[which(moralattenuation.logreg.1$type=='selfother'),'p'])`), but not significantly so in Sample 2, (*r*(`r moralattenuation.logreg.2[which(moralattenuation.logreg.2$type=='selfother'),'df']`) = `r formatrs(moralattenuation.logreg.2[which(moralattenuation.logreg.2$type=='selfother'),'r'])`, 95% CI [`r formatrs(moralattenuation.logreg.2[which(moralattenuation.logreg.2$type=='selfother'),'lci'])`, `r formatrs(moralattenuation.logreg.2[which(moralattenuation.logreg.2$type=='selfother'),'uci'])`], *p* = `r formatps(moralattenuation.logreg.2[which(moralattenuation.logreg.2$type=='selfother'),'p'])`), and this moral attenuation effect was similar compared to the self-report-only effects (Sample 1: *b* = `r round(comparebs.self.selfother.coefs.1['typeSelfOther:M_moralrelevance','Estimate'],2)`, 95% CI [`r round(confint(comparebs.self.selfother.1)['typeSelfOther:M_moralrelevance',1],2)`, `r round(confint(comparebs.self.selfother.1)['typeSelfOther:M_moralrelevance',2],2)`], *p* = `r formatps(comparebs.self.selfother.coefs.1['typeSelfOther:M_moralrelevance','Pr(>|t|)'])`; Sample 2: *b* = `r round(comparebs.self.selfother.coefs.2['typeSelfOther:M_moralrelevance','Estimate'],2)`, 95% CI [`r round(confint(comparebs.self.selfother.2)['typeSelfOther:M_moralrelevance',1],2)`, `r round(confint(comparebs.self.selfother.2)['typeSelfOther:M_moralrelevance',2],2)`], *p* = `r formatps(comparebs.self.selfother.coefs.2['typeSelfOther:M_moralrelevance','Pr(>|t|)'])`).

Finally, we predicted informant-reported priorities (from one randomly-selected informant) from aggregated informant-reported current levels. Because only two informants prioritized a goal to improve targets’ loyalty in Sample 2, this point estimate was implausibly large (β = 20.34, OR > 680,000; with very wide confidence intervals). Therefore, to avoid biasing the average odds ratios and other results reported here, we excluded this point estimate (for Sample 2 only). Overall, these odds ratios were descriptively stronger for nearly all traits, and were significantly larger compared to those obtained from self-reports only in Sample 1 (mean OR = `r round(exp(mean(compare.logreg.1$b_other)),2)`, *t*(`r self.selfother.logreg.t.1$parameter`) = `r round(self.other.logreg.t.1$statistic,2)`, *p* = `r formatps(self.other.logreg.t.1$p.value)`), but not in Sample 2 (mean OR = `r round(exp(mean(compare.logreg.2$b_other,na.rm=T)),2)`, *t*(`r self.other.logreg.t.2$parameter`) = `r round(self.other.logreg.t.2$statistic,2)`, *p* = `r formatps(self.other.logreg.t.2$p.value)`). Replicating the correlational results, informants’ change goals remained calibrated to their perceptions of targets’ current levels, even for more morally-relevant traits (for correlations with moral relevance, Sample 1: *r*(`r moralattenuation.logreg.1[which(moralattenuation.logreg.1$type=='other'),'df']`) = `r formatrs(moralattenuation.logreg.1[which(moralattenuation.logreg.1$type=='other'),'r'])`, 95% CI [`r formatrs(moralattenuation.logreg.1[which(moralattenuation.logreg.1$type=='other'),'lci'])`, `r formatrs(moralattenuation.logreg.1[which(moralattenuation.logreg.1$type=='other'),'uci'])`], *p* = `r formatps(moralattenuation.logreg.1[which(moralattenuation.logreg.1$type=='other'),'p'])`; Sample 2: *r*(`r moralattenuation.logreg.2[which(moralattenuation.logreg.2$type=='other'),'df']`) = `r formatrs(moralattenuation.logreg.2[which(moralattenuation.logreg.2$type=='other'),'r'])`, 95% CI [`r formatrs(moralattenuation.logreg.2[which(moralattenuation.logreg.2$type=='other'),'lci'])`, `r formatrs(moralattenuation.logreg.2[which(moralattenuation.logreg.2$type=='other'),'uci'])`], *p* = `r formatps(moralattenuation.logreg.2[which(moralattenuation.logreg.2$type=='other'),'p'])`). The odds ratios for more morally-relevant traits were larger when current levels and priorities were both informant-reported (vs. both self-reported) in Sample 1 (*b* = `r round(comparebs.self.other.coefs.1['typeOther:M_moralrelevance','Estimate'],2)`, 95% CI [`r round(confint(comparebs.self.other.1)['typeOther:M_moralrelevance',1],2)`, `r round(confint(comparebs.self.other.1)['typeOther:M_moralrelevance',2],2)`], *p* = `r formatps(comparebs.self.other.coefs.1['typeOther:M_moralrelevance','Pr(>|t|)'])`), but not in Sample 2 (*b* = `r round(comparebs.self.other.coefs.2['typeOther:M_moralrelevance','Estimate'],2)`, 95% CI [`r round(confint(comparebs.self.other.2)['typeOther:M_moralrelevance',1],2)`, `r round(confint(comparebs.self.other.2)['typeOther:M_moralrelevance',2],2)`], *p* = `r formatps(comparebs.self.other.coefs.2['typeOther:M_moralrelevance','Pr(>|t|)'])`).

*Figure S1.* Odds ratios representing the change in odds of prioritizing a given improvement (as one of their top three goals) for every 1 SD that a target was closer to the less desirable pole of that trait. Error bars depict the 95% confidence intervals. The traits are ordered from least to most morally relevant, based on the moral relevance norms for each respective sample.

# 6. Associations Between Moral Change Goals and Additional Individual Differences

## Measures

Descriptive statistics for these measures are reported in Table S3.

### Honesty-Humility

Honesty-Humility is the sixth major dimension of personality in the HEXACO model (Ashton, Lee, & de Vries, 2014), capturing preferences for fairness (e.g., “If I knew that I could never get caught, I would be willing to steal a million dollars” [r]), sincerity (e.g., “I wouldn’t pretend to like someone just to get that person to do favors for me”), greed avoidance (“Having a lot of money is not especially important to me”), and modesty (e.g., “I think that I am entitled to more respect than the average person is” [r]). Targets and informants rated the target’s Honesty-Humility using the 16-item subscale from the 100-item HEXACO Personality Inventory–Revised (Lee & Ashton, 2018; 1 = *Strongly disagree*, 5 = *Strongly agree*). We computed composites separately for self- and informant-rated Honesty-Humility.

### Moral elevation

Moral elevation describes the tendency to be emotionally moved and to feel inspired to be a better person when witnessing displays of moral excellence (Thomson & Siegel, 2017). Targets self-reported their trait moral elevation using the six “Engagement with Moral Beauty” items from the Engagement with Beauty Scale (Diessner, Solom, Frost, Parsons, & Davidson, 2008). However, we replaced mentions of “moral beauty” with “moral excellence,” as we thought this would improve the interpretability of the items (e.g., “When perceiving an act of moral excellence I feel emotional, it “moves me,” such as feeling a sense of awe, or wonder or excitement or admiration or upliftment”; 1 = *Very unlike me*, 7 = *Very much like me*).

### Impartial beneficence

The Oxford Utilitarianism Scale (Kahane et al., 2018) assesses individual differences in two dimensions of utilitarian thinking: instrumental harm (the willingness to harm innocent people for the greater good) and impartial beneficence (impartial concern for the greater good). Targets rated how much they endorsed five statements about the impartial promotion of people’s welfare (e.g., “It is morally wrong to keep money that one doesn’t really need if one can donate it to causes that provide effective help to those who will benefit a great deal”; 1 = *Strongly disagree*, 7 = *Strongly agree*).

### Moral foundations

Targets completed the 20-item version of the Moral Foundations Questionnaire (Graham et al., 2011). This instrument assesses the extent to which people use and endorse the moral foundations of Harm/Care, Fairness/Reciprocity, Ingroup/Loyalty, Authority/Respect, and Purity/Sanctity (four items each). Ten items are worded in terms of the moral relevance of each foundation (e.g., “Whether or not someone violated standards of purity and decency”; 0 = *Not at all relevant*, 5 = *Extremely relevant*), and ten items ask participants to indicate their agreement or disagreement with statements (e.g., “Compassion for those who are suffering is the most crucial virtue”; 0 = *Strongly disagree*, 5 = *Strongly agree*).

### Religiosity

Finally, targets completed a one-item measure of religiosity ("How religious are you?"; 1 = *Not at all religious*, 7 = *Extremely religious*).

```{r other moral correlates SEM, include=F}
x~~1*x
y~~1*y
w~~1*w
'

  EXT.S.modlist[[i]] <- gsub('wysyntax',wy.EXT.S,EXT.S.modlist[[i]])
}

# Remove the self-reported general morality predictor
# because we can't partial this variable out of itself
MCQ.GM.modlist <- MCQ.GM.modlist[-3]

# Combine all lists
all.modlist <- c(MCQ.GM.modlist,MCQ.F.modlist,AGR.R.modlist,
                 MCQ.H.modlist,MCQ.L.modlist,AGR.C.modlist,
                 CON.R.modlist,MCQ.P.modlist,AGR.T.modlist,
                 CON.P.modlist,anger.modlist,OPE.I.modlist,
                 NEG.E.modlist,NEG.D.modlist,EXT.E.modlist,
                 OPE.C.modlist,CON.O.modlist,NEG.A.modlist,
                 OPE.A.modlist,EXT.A.modlist,EXT.S.modlist)

#### Fit all SEMs and extract semi-partial correlations ####

create.spr.table <- function(dat){
  
  sprlist <- list()
  
  for(i in all.modlist){
    fit <- sem(i,data=dat,std.lv=T)
    spr <- parameterEstimates(fit)[which(parameterEstimates(fit)$lhs=='spr'),c('est','pvalue')]
    sprlist[[i]] <- spr
  }
  
  # negative variance issue resolved--it was just the BFI20 item
  # (applied a model constraint to deal with this)
  
  names(sprlist) <- names(all.modlist)
  spr.table <- ldply(sprlist)

  # Add significance stars
  spr.table$est <- formatrs(spr.table$est)
  spr.table[which(spr.table$pvalue<.05),'est'] <- paste0(spr.table[which(spr.table$pvalue<.05),'est'],'*')
  spr.table[which(spr.table$pvalue<.01),'est'] <- paste0(spr.table[which(spr.table$pvalue<.01),'est'],'*')
  spr.table[which(spr.table$pvalue<.001),'est'] <- paste0(spr.table[which(spr.table$pvalue<.001),'est'],'*')
  
  # Extract predictor
  spr.table$predictor <- sapply(strsplit(spr.table$.id, "_"), "[", 2)
  
  # Extract change goal
  spr.table$.id <- str_extract(spr.table$.id, ".+?(?=_)")
  
  # Long to wide
  spr.table.clean <- spr.table[,c('.id','predictor','est')]
  spr.table.clean <- reshape(spr.table.clean, idvar = ".id", timevar = "predictor", direction = "wide")
  
  names(spr.table.clean) <- gsub('est.','',names(spr.table.clean))
  
  spr.table.clean <- addtraitlabels(spr.table.clean)
  
  # Order table by average moral relevance
  spr.table.clean <- spr.table.clean[match(moralrelevance.avg$.id, spr.table.clean$.id),]
  
  spr.table.clean <- spr.table.clean[,c('Trait',all.predictors)]

  return(spr.table.clean)
  
}

spr.table.1 <- create.spr.table(dat.1)
spr.table.2 <- create.spr.table(dat.2)  # there were several convergence issues for purity. see below.
```

We were primarily interested in how strongly these individual differences correlated with highly morally-relevant change goals (i.e., goals to change general morality, fairness, respectfulness, honesty, loyalty, compassion, responsibility, purity, and trust), but we examined all change goals to provide information on discriminant validity. We used semi-partial correlations to estimate the unique association between each individual difference and change goal, controlling for current levels on each respective trait. For example, to estimate the semi-partial correlation between impartial beneficence and compassion change goals, we partialled out self-reported trait compassion. Here, we summarize the associations that replicated across both samples and that seemed theoretically noteworthy (but see Table S4 for all latent semi-partial correlations).

The results for moral elevation and the moral foundations were somewhat ambiguous. Although targets who self-reported a greater tendency to experience moral elevation also tended to report greater desires to increase on almost all moral traits (across both samples), they also tended to report goals to improve several non-moral traits (e.g., intellectual curiosity, energy level, productiveness), controlling for current levels on these traits. Thus, moral elevation may be linked with a general desire for self-improvement. The Purity foundation was especially strongly associated with goals to become more pure, but the other foundations showed fewer, less specific, or inconsistent associations with moral change goals.

Religiosity, impartial beneficence, and Honesty-Humility were more specifically linked with moral change goals across both samples. More religious targets tended to report greater desires to increase on compassion and loyalty. Impartial beneficence, the tendency to value impartially maximizing the greater good, also showed theoretically sensible associations with goals to become fairer and more compassionate. Finally, targets who self-reported being higher on Honesty-Humility tended to report greater goals to increase on honesty.

```{r reasons codings,include=F}
# Clean up reasons

clean.reasons.informant <- function(informant){
  #### Informant reasons ####
  reasons.ic <- table(informant$ic.rationale.benefit,informant$ic.top1)
  reasons.ic <- spread(data.frame(reasons.ic), Var1, Freq)
  reasons.ic$PercentTarget <- reasons.ic$`Benefit Target`/rowSums(reasons.ic[,2:3])
  
  reasons.ic$ic.n <- rowSums(reasons.ic[,2:4])
  
  reasons.ic$ic.PercentTarget <- reasons.ic$`Benefit Target`/reasons.ic$ic.n
  reasons.ic$ic.PercentInformant <- reasons.ic$`Benefit Self`/reasons.ic$ic.n
  reasons.ic$ic.PercentOther <- reasons.ic$`Other`/reasons.ic$ic.n
  
  # add empty rows for goals not mentioned
  notprioritized <- data.frame(Var2=setdiff(allgoals,reasons.ic$Var2))
  reasons.ic <- bind_rows(reasons.ic,notprioritized)
  
  return(reasons.ic)
  
}

reasons.ic.1 <- clean.reasons.informant(informant.1)
reasons.ic.2 <- clean.reasons.informant(informant.2)

clean.reasons.self <- function(dat){
  
  #### Target reasons ####
  
  reasons.tc <- table(dat$tc.rationale.benefit,dat$tc.top1)
  reasons.tc <- spread(data.frame(reasons.tc), Var1, Freq)
  reasons.tc$PercentTarget <- reasons.tc$`Benefit Self`/rowSums(reasons.tc[,2:3])
  
  reasons.tc$tc.n <- rowSums(reasons.tc[,2:4])
  reasons.tc$tc.PercentTarget <- reasons.tc$`Benefit Self`/reasons.tc$tc.n
  reasons.tc$tc.PercentOthers <- reasons.tc$`Benefit Others`/reasons.tc$tc.n
  reasons.tc$tc.PercentOther <- reasons.tc$`Other`/reasons.tc$tc.n
  
  # add empty rows for goals not mentioned
  notprioritized <- data.frame(Var2=setdiff(allgoals,reasons.tc$Var2))
  reasons.tc <- bind_rows(reasons.tc,notprioritized)
  
  return(reasons.tc)

}

reasons.tc.1 <- clean.reasons.self(dat.1)
reasons.tc.2 <- clean.reasons.self(dat.2)

merge.reasons <- function(reasons.tc,reasons.ic){
  
  reasons <- merge(reasons.tc[,c('Var2','tc.n','tc.PercentTarget',
                                     'tc.PercentOthers','tc.PercentOther')],
                     reasons.ic[,c('Var2','ic.n','ic.PercentTarget',
                                     'ic.PercentInformant','ic.PercentOther')],by='Var2',all=T)

  reasons[,c(3:5,7:9)] <- sapply(reasons[,c(3:5,7:9)],function(x){
    round(x*100,2)
  })

  reasons[is.na(reasons$tc.n),'tc.n'] <- 0
  reasons[is.na(reasons$ic.n),'ic.n'] <- 0

  reasons[which(reasons$tc.n==0),c('tc.PercentTarget',
                                     'tc.PercentOthers','tc.PercentOther')] <- NA

  reasons[which(reasons$ic.n==0),c('ic.PercentTarget',
                                     'ic.PercentInformant','ic.PercentOther')] <- NA

  reasons <- setorder(reasons,-tc.n)

  reasons <- cbind(reasons[1:5],NA,reasons[,6:9])
  
  reasons$Var2 <- as.character(reasons$Var2)
  
  return(reasons)
  
}
```

We explored whether informants wanted to change targets’ traits primarily for the targets’ sake, or their own sake. To do so, we coded open-ended responses to one question about targets’ and informants’ top change goal for the target: “Why do you want [target’s name] to change this aspect of your [their] personality?”. After removing invalid responses (e.g., “N/A” or responses that stated that they didn’t want the target to change), two research assistants coded whether targets’ responses ($n_{Sample1}$ = `r nrow(dat.1[!is.na(dat.1$tc.rationale.benefit),])`; $n_{Sample2}$ = `r nrow(dat.2[!is.na(dat.2$tc.rationale.benefit),])`) best reflected a concern for their own well-being or others’ well-being, and whether informants’ responses ($n_{Sample1}$ = `r nrow(informant.1[!is.na(informant.1$ic.rationale.benefit),])`; $n_{Sample2}$ = `r nrow(informant.2[!is.na(informant.2$ic.rationale.benefit),])`) best reflected a concern for the target’s well-being or the informant's own well-being. Coders selected “other” when the reason did not clearly reflect either category. The three categories were mutually-exclusive. Inter-rater agreement, as measured by the Cohen’s kappa [$\kappa$; Cohen, 1960], was moderate to substantial for both the informant (Sample 1: `r formatrs(kappa.ic.1)`; Sample 2: `r formatrs(kappa.ic.2)`) and target (Sample 1: `r formatrs(kappa.tc.1)`; Sample 2: `r formatrs(kappa.tc.2)`) codings. The first author resolved discrepancies between the two coders. The coding instructions and the de-identified open-ended responses are available in the OSF repository.

As shown in Table S11, the majority of informants’ reasons (Sample 1: `r round(reasons.ic.target.1,2)`%; Sample 2: `r round(reasons.ic.target.2,2)`%) reflected a concern for the targets’ well-being (e.g., “She is way too nice to people and I feel others can easily take advantage of her”), and relatively few reasons (Sample 1: `r round(reasons.ic.self.1,2)`%; Sample 2: `r round(reasons.ic.self.2,2)`) reflected the informant’s self-interest (e.g., “[target’s name] always sees the best in people - I, on the other hand, get annoyed with people easily and it’s hard to complain about someone to [target’s name]…”).

Similarly, the majority of targets’ reasons (Sample 1: `r round(reasons.tc.self.1,2)`%; Sample 2: `r round(reasons.tc.self.2,2)`%) reflected a concern for their own well-being (e.g., “I worry a lot about silly things, and it prevents me from getting the most happiness out of my life”), and very few reasons (Sample 1: `r round(reasons.tc.others.1,2)`%; Sample 2: `r round(reasons.tc.others.2,2)`%) reflected a concern for others’ well-being (e.g., “...I want to be there for my friends and family when they need someone”).

```{r odds,include=F}

moralimprovements <- c('More Moral','More Fair','More Respectful',
                       'More Honest','More Loyal','More Compassionate',
                       'More Responsible','More Trusting','More Pure')

nonmoralimprovements <- setdiff(desirablegoals,moralimprovements)

tc.reasons.test <- function(reasons.tc){
  
  reasons.tc.test <- reasons.tc[which(reasons.tc$Var2 %in% desirablegoals),c('Var2','Benefit Self','Benefit Others')]
  names(reasons.tc.test)[2:3] <- c('Benefit Target','Benefit Others')
  
  reasons.tc.test[which(reasons.tc.test$Var2 %in% moralimprovements),'Type'] <- 'Moral'
  reasons.tc.test[which(reasons.tc.test$Var2 %in% nonmoralimprovements),'Type'] <- 'Non-Moral'
  
  reasons.tc.test <- reasons.tc.test[,!names(reasons.tc.test) %in% 'Var2'] %>%
    group_by(Type) %>% 
    summarise_all(sum,na.rm=T)
  
  # Reorder so benefiting informant/others is the reference column
  reasons.tc.test <- reasons.tc.test[,c(1,3,2)]
  
  # Compute Fisher chi-square test
  or.tc.reasons <- fisher.test(reasons.tc.test[,2:3]) 
  
  return(or.tc.reasons)
  
}

or.tc.reasons.1 <- tc.reasons.test(reasons.tc.1)
or.tc.reasons.2 <- tc.reasons.test(reasons.tc.2)

ic.reasons.test <- function(reasons.ic){
  
  reasons.ic.test <- reasons.ic[which(reasons.ic$Var2 %in% desirablegoals),
                                  c('Var2','Benefit Self','Benefit Target')]
  
  names(reasons.ic.test)[2:3] <- c('Benefit Informant','Benefit Target')
  
  reasons.ic.test[which(reasons.ic.test$Var2 %in% moralimprovements),'Type'] <- 'Moral'
  reasons.ic.test[which(reasons.ic.test$Var2 %in% nonmoralimprovements),'Type'] <- 'Non-Moral'
  
  reasons.ic.test <- reasons.ic.test[,!names(reasons.ic.test) %in% 'Var2'] %>%
    group_by(Type) %>% 
    summarise_all(sum,na.rm=T)
  
  or.ic.reasons <- fisher.test(reasons.ic.test[,2:3]) 
  
  return(or.ic.reasons)
  
}

or.ic.reasons.1 <- ic.reasons.test(reasons.ic.1)
or.ic.reasons.2 <- ic.reasons.test(reasons.ic.2)
```

Finally, we explored whether these patterns varied depending on the moral relevance of the change goals. Because some change goals were rarely prioritized (see Table S11), for these low-frequency change priorities, the percentage of reasons that reflected a benefit to the self or to others were unlikely to be reliable estimates (e.g., if only 4 people prioritized a goal to become more honest, the estimates of 75% and 25% for reasons that benefit the self vs. benefit others would be very unreliable). This makes it unwise to examine the effects of moral relevance in a continuous way. Instead, we grouped the change goals into moral improvements (goals to be more moral, fair, respectful, honest, loyal, compassionate, responsible, trusting, and pure) and non-moral improvements (all other improvements), because there was a notable gap in moral relevance ratings between the least morally-relevant trait among the moral traits (Sample 1: $M_{Purity}$ = `r round(normtable.traits.1[which(normtable.traits.1$Trait=='Purity'),'M_moralrelevance'],2)`; Sample 2: $M_{Trust}$ = `r round(normtable.traits.2[which(normtable.traits.2$Trait=='Trust'),'M_moralrelevance'],2)`) and the most morally-relevant trait among the non-moral traits (Sample 1: $M_{Productiveness}$ = `r round(normtable.traits.1[which(normtable.traits.1$Trait=='Productiveness'),'M_moralrelevance'],2)`; Sample 2: $M_{Productiveness}$ = `r round(normtable.traits.2[which(normtable.traits.2$Trait=='Productiveness'),'M_moralrelevance'],2)`). 

We excluded the “Other” category and goals to change in the undesirable direction. Then, we computed the odds ratios (using Fisher’s exact test) for 2 (moral or non-moral improvement) $\times$ 2 (benefit target or benefit informant/others) contingency tables, separately for target- and informant-reported reasons. For the target-reported reasons, the odds of stating that the change would benefit others (vs. the target) were `r round(or.tc.reasons.1$estimate,2)` (Sample 1; 95% CI [`r round(or.tc.reasons.1$conf.int[1],2)`, `r round(or.tc.reasons.1$conf.int[2],2)`], *p* < .001) and `r round(or.tc.reasons.2$estimate,2)` (Sample 2; 95% CI [`r round(or.tc.reasons.2$conf.int[1],2)`, `r round(or.tc.reasons.2$conf.int[2],2)`], *p* < .001) times higher for moral (vs. non-moral) improvements. Similarly, for the informant-reported reasons, the odds of stating that the change would benefit the informant (vs. the target) were `r round(or.ic.reasons.1$estimate,2)` (Sample 1; 95% CI [`r round(or.ic.reasons.1$conf.int[1],2)`, `r round(or.ic.reasons.1$conf.int[2],2)`], *p* < .001) and `r round(or.ic.reasons.2$estimate,2)` (Sample 2; 95% CI [`r round(or.ic.reasons.2$conf.int[1],2)`, `r round(or.ic.reasons.2$conf.int[2],2)`], *p* < .001) times higher for moral (vs. non-moral) improvements. Therefore, both targets and informants wanted the target to make non-moral improvements for the target's own sake, but moral improvements for the sake of others.

# 8. Replication Study Establishing Generalizability to Older Adults

Several readers and audiences have expressed curiosity about whether the key finding (that people don’t particularly want to be more moral) generalizes beyond college students or young adults. To address this question, we conducted another preregistered replication with a sample of relatively older adults. Because we conducted this additional replication after the paper was accepted, this section has not been peer-reviewed. The data, code, materials, and preregistration can be accessed at https://osf.io/cbxjh.

## Method

We aimed to recruit 220 participants from Amazon’s Mechanical Turk, who were compensated with \$2 USD. We restricted participation to US-based participants who had a HIT approval rate ≥ 95%. To oversample for older adults, we recruited participants in three batches: 1) 50 participants who were between the ages of 45--55, 2) 50 participants who were age 55 or older, and 3) 120 participants with no age restrictions. Following our preregistered exclusion criteria, we excluded 23 incomplete responses and four participants who failed a simple attention check (“Please select the Agree button”). After these exclusions, Sample 3 comprised 222 targets (`r n.female.t.3` female, `r n.male.t.3` male, `r n.other.t.3` other or not disclosed) between the ages of `r minage.t.3` and `r maxage.t.3` years ($M_{age}$ = `r mage.t.3`, $SD_{age}$ = `r sdage.t.3`). Targets identified as White/Caucasian (*n* = `r n.white.t.3`), Black/African American (*n* = `r n.black.t.3`), Hispanic/Latino (*n* = `r n.hispanic.t.3`), Asian (*n* = `r n.asian.t.3`), or Other/Multiple (*n* = `r n.othereth.t.3`).

Targets self-reported their personality traits, change goals, and change goal priorities using the same measures described in the paper (along with additional exploratory measures, reported in the codebook). Targets also rated the moral relevance of the 42 items that were included in the change goals survey, using the same measures described in the paper. Thus, unlike the procedure in Samples 1 and 2, in which we obtained moral relevance ratings from participants who were not involved in the main study, in Sample 3, the moral relevance ratings were provided by the targets themselves. This provides person-specific moral relevance ratings, which we use in the within-person analyses reported below. In addition, unlike Samples 1 and 2, we did not recruit informants. All other data analytic procedures for the analyses we included in this replication study were identical to those reported in the main text.

## Results and Discussion

Descriptive statistics for the key measures are shown in Table S5.

```{r table S5,eval=T, include=F}
                      'M_change','SD_change','alpha_change',
                      'M_moralrelevance','SD_moralrelevance','mr.alpha')]

tableS5 <- cbind(tableS5[,c('Trait','M_trait','SD_trait','omega_trait')],NA,
                 tableS5[,c('M_change','SD_change','alpha_change')],NA,
                 tableS5[,c('M_moralrelevance','SD_moralrelevance','mr.alpha')])

# reorder from most to least morally-relevant

tableS5 <- setorder(tableS5,-M_moralrelevance)

write.csv(tableS5,'./Tables/tableS5.csv',row.names=F,na='')
```

```{r figure S2, eval=T, include=F}
create.figureS2.A <- function(perc.goals,sample){
      t.stackbardat <- melt(perc.goals[,c('.id','Trait','% same',
                                          '% increase','% decrease')],
                            id=c('.id','Trait'))
      
      t.stackbardat$type <- 'Self'
      
      t.stackbardat$variable <- as.character(t.stackbardat$variable)
      
      t.stackbardat[which(t.stackbardat$variable=='% same'),
                    'variable'] <- 'Want to Stay the Same'
      t.stackbardat[which(t.stackbardat$variable=='% increase'),
                    'variable'] <- 'Want Higher Levels'
      t.stackbardat[which(t.stackbardat$variable=='% decrease'),
                    'variable'] <- 'Want Lower Levels'
      
      # order from least to most morally-relevant (same order as Samples 1 & 2)
      moralorder <- factor(moralrelevance.avg$Trait)
      
      stackbardat <- t.stackbardat
      stackbardat[which(stackbardat$type=='Self'),
                  'value'] <- -1*stackbardat[which(stackbardat$type=='Self'),'value']
      
      label3 <- grobTree(textGrob('A', x=-.78,  y=1, hjust=0,
                                  gp=gpar(fontsize=18, fontface="bold")))
      
      all.stackbar.plot <- ggplot(stackbardat, 
                                  aes(y=value,x=Trait,fill=variable))+
        geom_bar(stat="identity",aes(fill=variable))+
        scale_fill_manual(name="",
                          values = c("steelblue","firebrick","grey"),
                          guide = guide_legend(reverse=T))+
        # theme(legend.position='bottom') +
        theme(legend.position='none') +
        coord_flip() +
        # geom_hline(yintercept=0) +
        theme(axis.line = element_line(color = 'black')) +
        xlab("")+
        ylab("Cumulative Percent of Goals") +
        theme(panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
              panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
              axis.text.y =  element_text(size=14,color='black'),
              axis.text.x =  element_text(size=14,color='black'),
              axis.title = element_text(size=14),
              plot.margin=unit(c(1.5,.5,0,0),"cm")) +
        scale_y_continuous(limits=c(-100.001,0),
                           breaks = seq(-100,0,by=20),
                           labels = seq(0,100,by=20),
                           expand=c(0,0)) +
        scale_x_discrete(limits=moralorder,expand=c(0,0)) +

}
```

Overall, targets showed a lower desire to change on traits that were more morally relevant, *r*(19) = `r formatrs(self.testmoralrelevance.3$estimate)`, 95% CI = [`r formatrs(self.testmoralrelevance.3$conf.int[1])`, `r formatrs(self.testmoralrelevance.3$conf.int[2])`], *p* < .001 (see Figure S2, Panel A). On the priorities measure (see Figure S2, Panel B), targets prioritized goals to become more energetic (`r round(top3summary.t.3[which(top3summary.t.3$Improvement=='More Energetic'),'Percent_self'],2)`%) about as often as goals to become less anxious (`r round(top3summary.t.3[which(top3summary.t.3$Improvement=='Less Anxious'),'Percent_self'],2)`%) and depressed (`r round(top3summary.t.3[which(top3summary.t.3$Improvement=='Less Depressed'),'Percent_self'],2)`%). In other words, compared to younger adults in Samples 1 and 2, goals to reduce anxiety and depression were relatively less important for these older adults. However, these older adults were still less inclined to prioritize more morally relevant improvements, *r*(19) = `r formatrs(self.moral.perc.3$estimate)`, 95% CI = [`r formatrs(self.moral.perc.3$conf.int[1])`, `r formatrs(self.moral.perc.3$conf.int[2])`], *p* < .001 (see Figure S2, Panel B). In other words, the finding that people are less inclined to improve moral traits is not only limited to college students.

*Figure S2.* Panel A shows the categorical summary of ratings on the change-goals scale for Sample 3. Stacked bars on the left show the percentage of targets who wanted higher levels, lower levels, or the same level of each trait. Panel B shows the percentage of targets who prioritized each trait as one of their top three most desired changes. Error bars depict 95% confidence intervals. For both panels, to facilitate visual comparison with Samples 1 and 2, we have ordered the traits from least to most morally relevant on the basis of the average of the moral relevance norms across Samples 1 and 2 (weighted equally). However, in the analyses for Sample 3, we used the moral relevance norms from Sample 3.

Figure S3 shows the latent correlations between self-reported current levels and change goals for each trait. In general, targets who reported having lower levels of a given trait wanted to increase more on that trait, mean *r* = `r formatrs(avgr.3)`. However, once again, the negative association between traits and change goals was smaller for more morally relevant traits, as shown by a strong positive association between moral-relevance scores and (Fisher *r*-to-*z* transformed) correlations between traits and change goals, *r*(19) = `r formatrs(test.attenuation.3$estimate)`, 95% CI [`r formatrs(test.attenuation.3$conf.int[1])`, `r formatrs(test.attenuation.3$conf.int[2])`], *p* = `r formatps(test.attenuation.3$p.value)`. In other words, the correlation between current levels and the desire to improve shifted from moderately negative for the least morally relevant traits to essentially zero for the most morally relevant traits.

*Figure S3.* Associations between self-reported current traits and change goals. The traits are ordered from least to most morally relevant on the basis of the moral-relevance norms for Sample 3. Error bars depict 95% confidence intervals.

### Do desirable trait levels explain why people do not want to be more moral?

```{r sample 3 within-person analyses, eval=T, include=F}

fit.mlms.3 <- function(datlong){
  mod.tc <- lmerTest::lmer(change_self~current_self.c+moral_relevance.c+
               (1 + current_self.c+moral_relevance.c|targetid),data=datlong,
               control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"))

  mod.tcp <- glmer(priorities_self ~ current_self.c + moral_relevance.c + 
            (0 + current_self.c + moral_relevance.c | targetid),
            family=binomial, data=datlong)
  
  mlm.list <- list(mod.tc,mod.tcp)
  
  # Get coefficients and p values
  
  # Extract coefficients from ind models
  mlm.coefs <- lapply(mlm.list,function(x){
    x <- data.frame(summary(x)$coefficients)
    names(x) <- gsub('r...t..','',names(x))
    names(x) <- gsub('r...z..','',names(x))
    x <- x[!row.names(x) %in% c('(Intercept)'),c('Estimate','P')]
    names(x)[2] <- 'pval'
    x$predictor <- row.names(x)
    x
  })
  
  names(mlm.coefs) <- c('mod.tc','mod.tcp')
  mlm.coefs <- ldply(mlm.coefs)
  
  # Get 95% CIs
  mlm.cis <- lapply(mlm.list,function(x){
    confint(x,method='Wald')
  })
  
  mlm.cis <- lapply(mlm.cis,function(x){
    x <- data.frame(x[which(row.names(x) %in% c('current_self.c','moral_relevance.c')),])
    x$predictor <- row.names(x)
    x
  })
  
  names(mlm.cis) <- c('mod.tc','mod.tcp')
  mlm.cis <- ldply(mlm.cis)
  names(mlm.cis)[2:3] <- c('lci','uci')
  
  # Match 95% CIs with point estimates
  mlm.coefs <- merge(mlm.coefs,mlm.cis,by=c('.id','predictor'))
  
  return(mlm.coefs)
  
}

mlm.coefs.3 <- fit.mlms.3(datlong.3)

#### Get within-person SDs for all variables ####

create.wpsd.table.3 <- function(datlong){
  # This function creates a table with all of the SDs needed
  # for standardized estimates
  
  # Fit null models
  null.list <- list()
  null.list <- lapply(c('current_self','change_self','moral_relevance'), 
                      function(var){
    form = paste(var,"~(1|targetid)")
    lme4::lmer(form, data=datlong)
  })
  
  null.order <- c('current_self','change_self','moral_relevance')
  
  wpsd.list <- lapply(null.list,get.wpsd)
  
  names(wpsd.list) <- null.order
  
  # convert list to table
  wpsd.table <- ldply(wpsd.list)
  
  names(wpsd.table)[1] <- 'predictor'
  names(wpsd.table)[2] <- 'SD_WP'
  
  return(wpsd.table)

}

wpsd.3 <- create.wpsd.table.3(datlong.3)

#### Standardize coefficients and clean up table ####

create.cleancoefs.3 <- function(mlm.coefs,wpsd){
  mlm.coefs$predictor <- gsub('.c','',mlm.coefs$predictor,fixed=T)
  
  mlm.coefs <- merge(mlm.coefs,wpsd,by='predictor',all.x=T)
  
  mlm.coefs[which(mlm.coefs$.id=='mod.tc'),'SD_WP_y'] <- wpsd[which(wpsd$predictor=='change_self'),'SD_WP']
  
  mlm.coefs[,c('SD_WP','SD_WP_y')] <- sapply(mlm.coefs[,c('SD_WP','SD_WP_y')],as.numeric)
  
  mlm.coefs[which(mlm.coefs$.id %in% c('mod.tc')),'type'] <- 'continuous'
  mlm.coefs[which(mlm.coefs$.id %in% c('mod.tcp')),'type'] <- 'priorities'
  
  # standardize beta coefficients for continuous change goals against
  # within-person SD of both X & Y
  mlm.coefs[which(mlm.coefs$type=='continuous'),
            c('est_std','lci_std','uci_std')] <- sapply(
              mlm.coefs[which(mlm.coefs$type=='continuous'),c('Estimate','lci','uci')],
            function(x){
              x*mlm.coefs[which(mlm.coefs$type=='continuous'),'SD_WP']/
                mlm.coefs[which(mlm.coefs$type=='continuous'),'SD_WP_y']})
    
  # standardize beta coefficients for priorities against within-person SD of X
  mlm.coefs[which(mlm.coefs$type=='priorities'),
            c('est_std','lci_std','uci_std')] <- sapply(
              mlm.coefs[which(mlm.coefs$type=='priorities'),c('Estimate','lci','uci')],
            function(x){
              x*mlm.coefs[which(mlm.coefs$type=='priorities'),'SD_WP']})
    
  # exponentiate standardized coefficients for odds ratios
  mlm.coefs[,c('est_clean','lci_clean','uci_clean')] <- mlm.coefs[,c('est_std','lci_std','uci_std')]
  
  mlm.coefs[which(mlm.coefs$type=='priorities'),
            c('est_clean','lci_clean','uci_clean')] <- sapply(
  mlm.coefs[which(mlm.coefs$type=='priorities'),
            c('est_std','lci_std','uci_std')],exp)
  
  # tidy up
  mlm.coefs[,c('est_clean','lci_clean','uci_clean')] <- sapply(mlm.coefs[,c('est_clean','lci_clean','uci_clean')],function(x){round(x,2)})
  
  mlm.coefs$pval <- round(mlm.coefs$pval,3)
  
  mlm.coefs <- mlm.coefs[,c('type','predictor','est_clean','lci_clean','uci_clean','pval')]
  
  return(mlm.coefs)
  
}

clean.coefs.3 <- create.cleancoefs.3(mlm.coefs.3,wpsd.3)

```

Finally, we used multi-level modeling to examine whether people are less motivated to change more morally-relevant traits, controlling for their perceptions of their current levels. We used the same approach described above (see Section 3), except that we used person-specific measures of moral relevance (rather than aggregate moral relevance scores), which were within-person-centered. Once again, these within-person analyses showed that current levels and moral relevance scores independently predicted lowered change goals for both the continuous and priority-based measures. In other words, targets were less inclined to change on traits that they considered to be more morally relevant (β = `r clean.coefs.3[which(clean.coefs.3$type=='continuous' & clean.coefs.3$predictor=='moral_relevance'),'est_clean']`, 95% CI [`r clean.coefs.3[which(clean.coefs.3$type=='continuous' & clean.coefs.3$predictor=='moral_relevance'),'lci_clean']`, `r clean.coefs.3[which(clean.coefs.3$type=='continuous' & clean.coefs.3$predictor=='moral_relevance'),'uci_clean']`], *p* < .001), even controlling for current levels (β = `r clean.coefs.3[which(clean.coefs.3$type=='continuous' & clean.coefs.3$predictor=='current_self'),'est_clean']`, 95% CI [`r clean.coefs.3[which(clean.coefs.3$type=='continuous' & clean.coefs.3$predictor=='current_self'),'lci_clean']`, `r clean.coefs.3[which(clean.coefs.3$type=='continuous' & clean.coefs.3$predictor=='current_self'),'uci_clean']`], *p* < .001). They were also less inclined to prioritize improving traits that they considered to be more morally relevant (OR = `r clean.coefs.3[which(clean.coefs.3$type=='priorities' & clean.coefs.3$predictor=='moral_relevance'),'est_clean']`, 95% CI [`r clean.coefs.3[which(clean.coefs.3$type=='priorities' & clean.coefs.3$predictor=='moral_relevance'),'lci_clean']`, `r clean.coefs.3[which(clean.coefs.3$type=='priorities' & clean.coefs.3$predictor=='moral_relevance'),'uci_clean']`], *p* < .001), even controlling for current levels (OR = `r clean.coefs.3[which(clean.coefs.3$type=='priorities' & clean.coefs.3$predictor=='current_self'),'est_clean']`, 95% CI [`r clean.coefs.3[which(clean.coefs.3$type=='priorities' & clean.coefs.3$predictor=='current_self'),'lci_clean']`, `r clean.coefs.3[which(clean.coefs.3$type=='priorities' & clean.coefs.3$predictor=='current_self'),'uci_clean']`], *p* < .001).
